title: Swans AFLW star says club's men's and women's players closer than ever
text:
Believing Sydney's men's and women's teams are closer than before, AFLW star Cynthia Hamilton has described the embattled club's resilience amid turmoil as "actually beautiful".

Hamilton is urging fans to continue their support, vowing the Swans won't disappoint on the field in Sunday's Sydney derby against rivals GWS at Henson Park.

The Swans women play in the Harbour City for the first time since the SCG double-header in round two, having played a home game in Coffs Harbour in round three.

Swans offer timely reminder of what 'Bloods' culture is meant to look like Many questions were asked about Sydney's famed culture in the wake of the Pullman Hotel scandal. As the finals got underway, the players showed exactly what it is supposed to look like on the field.

Fans came out in force at the SCG in the immediate aftermath of the men's Pullman Hotel scandal, with a crowd of 16,672 turning up for the victory over Essendon.

The attendance more than doubled Sydney's previous highest crowd for a home AFLW game.

In contrast, the men's team recorded its lowest SCG crowd of the season, just 30,058 fans watched them beat North Melbourne.

Star players Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner and Nick Blakey — All-Australian contenders before they were banned from being selected — are among the five serving club-imposed bans.

Important tagger James Jordon and defender Riley Bice are the other Swans who won't play again this season.

Errol Gulden (right) has been getting Sydney's men's and women's players together for breathwork sessions. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

As the men's team aims to rebuild respect for the famed "Bloods" culture, Hamilton says the club have come together even over the smallest of details.

"This has honestly brought us closer. We're doing breathwork in the morning together, we're doing little things," Hamilton said.

"Errol Gulden's been flicking the message [about breathwork] across to join both teams together as an opportunity to come closer.

"The boys have been bloody awesome. They've really brought the two groups together.

" In light of what's happened, it's actually kind of beautiful how the club has reacted. I would say we're closer than what we were before. "

As a healthy contingent followed the women's to Whitten Oval last week, the men's team enjoyed renewed support for their 53-point qualifying final upset of reigning premiers Brisbane and played in front of 37,261 fans at the SCG.

"When you look on the weekend, and you see the support the boys are getting, and then vice versa when we were at the SCG as well, it just shows how special the Bloods bond is and that the culture is there," Hamilton said.

"Keep getting around us, keep showing up, and we won't disappoint, hopefully."

GWS forward Tarni Evans also threw her weight behind the Swans, after urging fans to support the AFLW fixture at the SCG last month.

Sydney's AFLW side has received a mountain of support from both inside and outside the club. (Getty Images: Kelly Defina)

The 14th-placed Giants are looking to retain derby bragging rights and bounce back from a dour 31-point away loss to the Lions, taking a three-game losing streak to Henson Park.

Sydney is also licking its wounds after a 27-point defeat to the Western Bulldogs, leaving the Swans fifth after a first loss of the season.

Both sides have claimed two wins from four previous derbies in the women's league.

"This weekend, this is such a great opportunity in women's sport, to get out and support it," Evans said.

"Getting people to the game is unreal and that's what we want.

"This weekend will be another testament to that, a great game of footy to watch."

AAP

title: Opals remain perfect at World Cup despite 2am fire alarm wake-up call
text:
Australia has made it two from two at the FIBA Women's Basketball World Cup with an 87-71 win over Türkiye in Berlin.

It was an improved performance by the Opals after their opening 70-54 victory over Puerto Rico, leaving Sandy Brondello's side set to progress to the knockout stages.

New captain Ezi Magbegor was instrumental in the second straight victory with 21 points on 10/14 shooting, leading the way with able support from Steph Talbot's 17 points.

It was an impressive performance considering the unceremonious 2am wake-up call the teams received when a fire alarm went off at the team hotel.

Ezi Magbegor led the way with 21 points. (Supplied: FIBA)

The players and coaches all had to evacuate the hotel before going back inside the building about an hour later.

There was no fire, someone had pushed the emergency alarm button in the elevator, according to Brondello.

"That's a what-if situation, isn't it?" Brondello said.

"Now we have that in our toolbox. Never done that before."

The interrupted sleep did not seem to hurt the Opals in the first game of the day that tipped at 11:30am local time.

"It was kind of crazy. Just kind of happened," Australia forward Ezi Magbegor said.

"Knowing that it's out of our control, so just getting back to sleep and waking up. No-one was going to feel sorry for us."

Turkish coach Andrea Masson said he and his players got about three hours of sleep because of the alarm.

"They had a really bad night last night," Masson said.

"That's not an excuse, but that's the reality."

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

ABC/AP

title: Author's YA book partly inspired by experience as sex educator in schools
text:
Surya feels like a bad queer. When an ice cream man misgenders them, they stay silent.

Kamalakanthan has said Bad Queer is about queer "futures & the worlds we're building together". (Supplied: Allen & Unwin)

"I pray for a sharper tongue," they think when a classmate harasses them for not looking like either a boy or a girl.

Surya is the protagonist of Bad Queer, a young adult novel-in-verse written by London-based Gayathiri Kamalakanthan and illustrated by Chicago artist Chi Nwosu.

Coming into their final year at school, Surya has come out to their parents, who are queer and non-binary, and their close friend Maha, but not to everyone.

They're also yet to have their first romantic relationship.

"I would really like to like someone. But I know I can't force it," they reflect.

'Poetry and illustration are a beautiful match'

Throughout Bad Queer, Nwosu's line drawings help develop Surya's journey of self-acceptance.

One of Nwosu's favourite illustrations from the book captures the "vast aloneness when you're not fully seen". (Supplied: Allen & Unwin)

Sometimes the illustrations capture a detail from the text, like Surya's hands writing in their journal or the tiles in a family game of Scrabble.

Elsewhere, they take us into Surya's internal emotions, like a flurry of stars and swirls that surround the text as Surya practices deep breathing in a bathroom stall.

"I think poetry and illustration are a beautiful match because they're both asking the reader to interpret and really be part of co-creating the story," Kamalakanthan says of the book's unusual format.

Nwosu, a Black, non-binary, queer Nigerian American artist and designer, relates to how Surya feels connected to their ancestors and how they're searching for representation of their queer and non-binary self in Tamil culture.

"I find myself looking towards Igbo history in a similar way," Nwosu says.

"I want to know where are the others? Where are the outliers? How did folks treat people who were different or had a different orientation towards the world?

" [Surya's story] reflected my own experience as someone who didn't fit neatly into a binary. "

Nwosu has created works for an exhibition celebrating their local basketball team, the Chicago Bulls. (Supplied: Allen & Unwin)

One aspect of the project Nwosu particularly enjoyed was learning about Tamil symbolism and incorporating it respectfully into their work.

"A lot of my own art incorporates cultural and spiritual symbols as a way to learn, remember and honour my Igbo culture and the histories of global solidarity and queer solidarity," they say.

Finding themselves on stage

Surya's life changes when, on a whim, they audition for their school's youth theatre.

"It's as if this one audition is a mini protest against all the times I've said nothing" they think.

The group, led by the enthusiastic Mr Ali, proves a safe space for Surya to explore and embrace their identity.

In this new environment, Surya soon befriends Akhil, who proudly wears a "GAY AF" badge and Sade, who gives Surya a worry stone to soothe their pre-audition anxiety.

Then there's Blessing, a newcomer with a "perfectly crooked" smile. Surya is soon smitten.

Surya develops feelings for Blessing, a Ghanaian British boy interested in acting and photography. (Supplied: Allen & Unwin)

Kamalakanthan says their own experiences working in the theatre, including writing a play, Period Parrrty, were "foundational" for them.

"I gained confidence to really step into the intersection of my Tamilness and genderqueerness," they say.

"There's something about theatre being a communal act. You're not just writing in a room by yourself. You're in rehearsal rooms, trading mood boards, figuring out a shared vision with a director and cast, and that collective imagining really opened up my confidence."

'I wanted him to get things wrong and keep trying'

As Surya's relationship with Blessing develops, they gain the confidence to live as their true self.

While Blessing is kind and empathetic, it's also a journey for him to embrace being in a queer relationship.

Nwosu's illustrations catch the moment Surya sees their crush Blessing smile: "Butterflies riot in my belly." (Supplied: Allen & Unwin)

"Because of the binary world we live in, [Blessing] has a difficult time understanding Surya's transness," Kamalakanthan says.

"I wanted him to get things wrong and keep trying and not shy away from doing his own thinking and research about what he doesn't understand yet."

Kamalakanthan says the arc of the relationship was inspired by their previous work as a sex and relationships educator.

"I noticed students were often more fluent in naming sexual harm than articulating consent and the type of touch they might be comfortable with," they say.

"I wanted characters in Bad Queer to model those exact conversations: fumbling, hesitant and laughing nervously through the words … and importantly working out their boundaries before any touch happens.

"There's so much in books and TV about sexual violence, which is of course an important topic to understand.

"But I also wanted to write consensual, caring relationships. We need templates for those conversations too."

'Stories that I really longed for as a young person'

Kamalakanthan and Nwosu hope Bad Queer strikes a chord with young people coming to terms with their gender identity and sexual orientation.

"As a young person, I felt like I didn't quite have the words to describe the feeling of queerness that I had inside," Nwosu says.

"To understand what it means to find dignity for yourself as a queer and genderqueer person and to learn to accept the parts of yourself that maybe make other people uncomfortable was one of the profound takeaways from the book for me.

" It was incredible to work on a book intended for young people and to know they will have these stories that I really longed for as a young person. "

This illustration accompanies a moment of release for Surya: "And I didn't realise how hard/I was clenching my fists/Till I let go." (Supplied: Allen & Unwin)

Kamalakanthan says they want to present a different kind of narrative around queer and trans youth, who often don't get support or understanding from their parents.

"I wanted to write a family where being trans is incidental alongside the usual messiness and tenderness of any family," they say,.

"Surya's parents won't always have all the answers, but they're people who Surya knows are safe enough to express worries and anxieties to, including if anything unsafe or harmful is going on.

"For a lot of queer people I know, our teenage years were spent hiding, feeling unsafe and managing how we were perceived, rather than discovering the fullness of who we could be.

"I want the characters in my stories to have the teenage adolescence a lot of us didn't get to have, that I hope young people get to have now."

Bad Queer is published by Allen & Unwin.

title: Review finds maternity unit problems persist at Toowoomba Hospital
text:
Longstanding issues at Toowoomba Hospital's troubled maternity unit remain unresolved, an independent review of the ward has said.

The assurance review of the unit, released today, found that while some changes were underway, several areas, including complaint processes, still needed fixing.

Queensland Health commissioned the review in February after years of complaints from mothers and families about maternity services at the major regional hospital.

Most recently, a Toowoomba mother revealed footage that showed her support person being unnecessarily removed from the birth of her son.

Toowoomba maternity concerns A confrontation caught on body-worn security footage in the halls of the Toowoomba Hospital maternity unit highlights concerns raised by local mothers.

A panel wrote the report, which was prepared by independent experts who examined Darling Downs Health's response to five previous reviews and investigations into the service since 2018 and the 117 recommendations made.

The experts highlight how long the report took to finalise: an Internal Maternity Services Review Report was commissioned in August 2018 but was not received by the chief executive until October last year.

Focus on complaints

A significant portion of the review focused on how complaints were handled at the hospital, particularly on maternity outcomes since January 1, 2025.

It found the hospital had no dedicated maternity complaints service and described "barriers to raising concerns, poor visibility of complaint pathways, dissatisfaction with responses, poor communication, lack of follow-up, and a perception that complaints did not lead to meaningful resolution or change."

"In particular, concerns raised in real time during care were sometimes experienced as dismissed, minimised or redirected into formal processes without meaningful response."

The review found policy change was "early in its lifecycle" and not yet embedded into routine practice at the maternity ward.

The review into the maternity service assessed the recommendations from five separate reports and investigations dating back to 2018. (ABC Southern Qld: Brandon Long)

"The service is still transitioning from a reactive model of governance to a more proactive, evidence-based approach," the report said.

The panellists identified a "significant risk" that the specific details from the 117 previous recommendations may have been "inadvertently overlooked" when being broadly summarised in Darling Downs Health' Master Action Plan.

Director-general of Queensland Health David Rosengren said Darling Downs Health was considering the opportunities identified by the review to strengthen the complaints process and support community confidence in maternity outcomes "as a matter of priority".

"Queensland Health values the opportunity to improve its processes and services, and I thank staff and consumers for their participation in the assurance review."

Review accepted, new director appointed

Darling Downs Health chief executive Annette Scott said the hospital did not want to hide from its shortcomings and was committed to improving how it engages with women and families.

Annette Scott says she is committed to improving the maternity service. (ABC Southern Qld: Brandon Long)

"How we used to do engagement is no longer meeting all the needs of this community," Ms Scott said.

" We don't shy away from it. We are ready to work with any women who want to come forward. "

She acknowledged the deficits in the complaints process highlighted by the review and said any complaints that were lost were "unacceptable".

"I don't want that on my watch at all. If things are getting lost then we need to learn from that," Ms Scott said.

"It's my job and my commitment to this community that we'll do our darnedest to ensure that we'll get better at this."

The review also highlighted that Toowoomba Hospital's recently appointed midwife guide position, a dedicated support role installed after a series of complaints, was not well integrated with the mainstream complaints process.

Ms Scott said a new director of obstetrics had also been appointed and noted that vacancies in midwifery roles had dropped from 14 per cent last October to 2 per cent currently.

It comes after several senior staff from the maternity unit took leave last year and two directors of obstetrics resigned within weeks of each other.

Separate to the independent maternity assurance review, Ms Scott confirmed a review was being undertaken into a serious incident at the maternity service.

The incident was categorised as causing "death or likely permanent harm which is not reasonably expected as an outcome of health care", under Queensland Health's Clinical Incident Management Guidelines.

title: Bathla stands down 213 staff, secures two-week funding extension
text:
The debt-ridden Bathla Group has reached a short-term funding agreement with five of its lenders which will continue its survival for another two weeks.

The property developer's administrator, Teneo, says this funding will allow construction to continue on those lenders' construction projects.

However, construction on other projects will be suspended today, resulting in approximately 213 employees being stood down.

The group has around 350 employees, many of whom are on working visas, who found out their fate this morning at an all-staff meeting.

Administrators would not reveal which lenders had provided the temporary lifeline or which of Bathla's 45 active projects were still going ahead.

However, the ABC understands the five lenders include La Trobe, PAG, Centuria Bass and Ray White Capital.

The funding amount is between $3 and $5 million.

Bathla's administrators have stood down 200 of its staff. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Sites belonging to lenders who did not provide funding to Bathla's administrators have been suspended, the ABC understands.

Those lenders will need to find a new building licence if they wish to take over the sites and pay subcontractors directly, it is understood.

Last week the ABC confirmed that a 312-apartment block development in Pemulwuy in Sydney's west is going ahead after the lender PAG committed to continue paying contractors directly.

An 82-apartment block in Richmond and an estate in Vineyard in western Sydney are also going ahead, it is understood.

A 68-unit block in Sydney's Castle Hill is not part of the rescue.

Administrators have received funding for some projects. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Administrator Stephen Longley said today that although funding had been secured, they needed more if the group were to be able to keep functioning in two weeks.

"The arrangements agreed today allow us to provide the central support required for construction to continue on projects associated with the lenders participating in the funding package," Mr Longley said in a statement.

"Significant work remains to secure the funding required to progress and ultimately complete all projects currently under construction.

"We will continue to work closely with lenders and other key stakeholders to pursue those arrangements."

Embattled developer

Bathla plunged into administration at the end of August after being unable to pay its $3.4 billion in debts.

Teneo managed to reach an 11th-hour funding deal last Thursday to meet Bathla's payroll obligations that day, after revealing that some staff had not been paid for eight weeks.

Administrators estimate supporting construction would cost the business about $1 million to $1.3 million a week, depending on which projects continue.

Bathla is one of Sydney's biggest residential property developers, with a large pipeline of housing projects and land holdings across the region.

Its administration has left the fate of 200 projects across NSW in jeopardy, with roughly 2,000 homes under construction and another 13,000 in its development pipeline.

Administrators had tried tapping existing lenders for extra funds and in late August asked the New South Wales government for a $20 million lifeline to keep the business afloat.

However, the state government refused to offer any bailout money.

Bathla Group is on the rocks. (ABC News: John Gunn)

The ABC previously reported on Bathla's tenuous debt position revealed during its first creditors meeting held on Friday.

Bathla Group owes known creditors about $3.4 billion, based on preliminary figures, with the vast majority, $3.08 billion, owed to secured lenders.

Bathla also owes about $145 million to the Australian Taxation Office, $42 million in land tax and $130 million to other unsecured creditors.

About $4 million is owed to employees for wages and superannuation.

Administrators also put the preliminary stated value of Bathla's 219 sites at about $4.9 billion.

title: Labuschagne retained for South Africa Test series despite pressure
text:
Marnus Labuschagne will travel to South Africa for next month's Test tour of South Africa after being named in a 16-man squad.

There have been calls for the number three to be dropped after more than three years without a Test century, but the 32-year-old has kept his spot for the tour despite being left out of the side for six ODIs leading up to the Test series.

Australia's men's team will play three ODIs against Zimbabwe in Harare followed by three more 50-over games against South Africa in Durban, Johannesburg and Potchefstroom before the Tests in Durban (October 9-13), Gqeberha (October 18-22) and Cape Town (October 27-31).

Chairman of selectors George Bailey said a pure focus on red-ball cricket "may be a benefit" for Labuschagne.

"Not shying away from the fact we'd like some more runs from Marn, that's clear," he said.

Is Marnus Labuschagne running out of luck? After spending years as one of the luckiest Test cricketers in the game, Marnus Labuschagne's fortunes appear to BE turning and, unfortunately for him, so has his form.

"But we're also confident he can still make a positive contribution to that squad."

Labuschagne has never played a Test in South Africa, where he was born and spent the first 10 years of his life.

Big-hitting Cooper Connolly, spinner Matthew Kuhnemann and seamer Michael Neser, another South Africa-born Australian, have been added to the group that contested the second Test against Bangladesh in Mackay last month.

Bailey said Connolly, who bowls part-time spin, had been selected primarily for his batting, with Josh Inglis the only other batter in the squad outside the XI from the Bangladesh series.

Both players have traditionally batted in the middle order in first-class cricket.

It leaves the team without a huge number of options for change if the batting line-up continues to struggle.

"Our batting group in its entirety, not just Marn, probably hasn't been functioning as successfully as we would like," he admitted.

"But we've continued to win a lot of Test matches over that period and that ultimately is the key, scoring more runs than the opposition."

Connolly, 23, is one of three players in the squad under 30, along with 29-year-old Kuhnemann and 27-year-old all-rounder Cameron Green, with the latter the only incumbent in the team.

It raises concerns about an impending transition as the majority of the team ages out with little Test experience in younger players behind them.

"Age is a big focus for some, performance I think is important," Bailey said.

"We're confident around where that group's at and also over the ensuing months years as the transitions occur, be that through performance or players dropping out of formats, there'll be good people that are well placed to come in and perform in whichever team that is."

title: Kids sport costing families more than $4,500 a year for each child
text:
For Rockhampton parents Aaron and Paula Harmsworth, keeping three children involved in multiple sports comes with a growing price tag.

"It's something we talk about regularly because we do look at the bank balance and go, 'Geez, we're spending a lot of money here,'" Mr Harmsworth said.

"But we counteract that pretty quickly with: 'There is no price tag on what the kids learn through sport.'

"The people they meet, the places they go, and the different traits they learn … respect and resilience, they're probably two of the biggest key components."

Siblings Sienna, Indy and Jace Harmsworth are all competing at representative level in a range of sports. (ABC Capricornia: Aaron Kelly)

New research has found the average annual total cost for a child to play in a community sport competition is $4,567 a year, considerably higher than previously reported numbers.

The Cost of Sport study, commissioned by the Australian Sports Commission and undertaken by researchers from Federation University, also found adults were forking out $2,894 per year for themselves to play.

Researchers investigated a wide range of expenses, including registration, equipment, uniforms, coaching, travel, accommodation and lost parental income due to sport commitments.

Sienna Harmsworth has earned selection in Queensland teams in three sports this year. (Supplied: The Cathedral College)

For the Harmsworth family, those costs quickly add up.

Their children, Jace, 17, Sienna, 15, and Indy, 13, have represented their city, region and state in various sports, with Sienna making Queensland teams in hockey, netball and touch football in 2026.

Already this year, sport has taken the central Queensland family from Hobart to Darwin and plenty of places in between.

"We have to map out our year and generally we have to be pretty organised," Mr Harmsworth said.

"This year alone we've done Goulburn, Gold Coast, Mackay, Brisbane, and then back to Brisbane, Hobart, Mackay, Cairns, Melbourne, Gold Coast again, Mackay again, Brisbane, Coffs Harbour, Darwin, back to Brisbane, back to Mackay, Cairns and Hervey Bay."

This year alone Sienna Harmsworth has pulled on the maroon jersey in hockey, netball and touch football. (Supplied: Paula Harmsworth)

It all adds up for families

The study's lead researcher, Rochelle Eime, said previous research had tended to focus on registration fees, while her team captured the broader financial commitment families made to sport.

"It seems like a really high number, but when you start looking at all the different categories, it all stacks up," Professor Eime said.

" You've got $1,400 for coaching for an individual sport on average, $1,000 lost to parent income to travel, another $700 for tournament or competition accommodation fees, $500 for travel. "

Rochelle Eime says travel, coaching and other costs can quickly add up for families involved in community sport. (Supplied: Rochelle Eime)

Mr Harmsworth said the sacrifices for his family were not just monetary.

"You accrue leave and, all of a sudden, you're using your leave on a sporting trip," he said.

" You certainly look at what the word family holiday means now and that generally means a sporting holiday. "

New research has found the average annual cost of community sport for a child is more than $4,500. (ABC News: Jonathon Gul)

The study surveyed about 5,500 sport participants across Australia, including children and adults.

It found the overall cost for children to play sport was similar in regional and remote areas compared with metropolitan areas.

But regional children faced higher travel and accommodation costs, while metropolitan families paid more for coaching and registration fees.

Equipment such as headgear and boots can add to the cost of playing community sport. (ABC News: Jen Browning)

Entry-level participation was much cheaper, averaging $1,161 a year for children, while the average cost for adults was $1,200.

Individual sports were also found to be more expensive than team sports.

"What we're seeing is most people and families aren't just entry-level sport participants," Professor Eime said.

"As soon as you get into that later childhood, you do need to travel to play in competitions and that all adds up."

Researchers say the cost of community sport rises as children progress into competitive and representative sport. (AAP: Joe Castro)

Keeping kids in the game

Professor Eime said sporting clubs and organisations were already finding ways to ensure cost did not become a barrier to participation.

Some were repurposing equipment and uniforms, while many supported state government voucher programs, which in Queensland can reduce the cost of sport by up to $200 per child.

"The value of community sport is so great for our children in terms of their youth development and social connectedness, a whole range of different life skills they get from playing sport," Professor Eime said.

A shot at goal can come with a growing price tag for sporting families. (AAP: Dave Hunt)

"If we highlight what the true costs are, and they are much higher than what previous research has shown, we need to actually do something about it because everyone should have the chance to play community sport."

Danya Hodgetts, a senior researcher at CQUniversity and an expert in community sport, who was not involved in the study, said the findings reflected what many regional parents already knew: that the cost of getting their children off screens and involved in sport extended well beyond registration fees.

Danya Hodgetts says community sport provides benefits that extend well beyond the playing field. (Supplied: CQUniversity)

"It's a really tricky situation because it is important that, while we talk about the cost of sport, we also talk about the value of sport because we know sport is valuable," Dr Hodgetts said.

"It builds good humans, keeps kids out of trouble, it keeps them occupied, it keeps them healthy and it also, particularly in regional areas, it's our village.

"Sporting clubs are the networks that parents and kids rely on to help get through daily life, not just inside sport, but outside of sport as well."

More sporting road trips are ahead for the Harmsworth family, with the September school holidays bringing another round of travel. (ABC Capricornia: Aaron Kelly)

For the Harmsworth family, finding ways to keep those costs under control has become part of playing the sporting game.

Mr Harmsworth said their caravan had become one of their biggest money savers.

"One of our saving graces is the caravan and we take it everywhere we go," he said.

"You also need to book early and in advance in a lot of cases, particularly your bigger sporting carnivals."

title: Young tractor drivers follow in grandfathers' tracks to keep event alive
text:
At the ages of 10 and 11, most children are still learning to ride a bike.

However, 10-year-old Jackson Kovac and 11-year-old Angus McKenzie are already behind the wheel of powerful tractors.

The boys were the youngest competitors at the Tractor Restoration and Appreciation Club of Sunraysia's (TRACS) annual tractor pull at Red Cliffs on the weekend.

Each year, tractor enthusiasts gather in Red Cliffs to put their machines to the test by pulling a weighted sled along a 100-metre-long track.

It was Jackson's debut on the track, having eagerly awaited his chance to enter after seeing his mate Angus make his debut last year.

Jackson has been driving his grandfather's tractor for about two years and has had many practice runs at home using the family's own sled.

Jackson Kovac standing between the two tractors he drove during his first tractor pull. (ABC News: Lua Ikenasio)

At this year's event, he competed behind the wheel of two different tractors.

When asked about what he enjoyed most about being on a tractor, his answer was simple.

"It's just the joy of driving and it's just fun," he said.

For Jackson, competing in tractor pulls is a family tradition.

His grandfather Ross Kovac has been involved in tractor pulls for about 30 years and was behind the wheel of one at an even younger age than Jackson.

"I was born and bred on the farm, so I was driving tractors at the age of probably four," he said.

"We've been in tractor pulls for a long time ... originally it was out there at Coomealla, then they folded up and then this TRACS club started back in the late 90s, so we joined up and we've been in the game ever since."

Ross Kovac and his grandson Jackson, who was one of the youngest competitors in this year's tractor pull. (ABC News: Lua Ikenasio)

Now, Mr Kovac is watching his grandchildren do the same.

"I'm very proud. It's great to see them," he said.

For Angus, the love of machines has also been inherited from his grandfather, Alan McKenzie.

"[I was] just mucking around with my pop in his garage," he said.

"I got into it, just driving around the garage, helping him out."

Alan McKenzie competing at the 2026 TRACS tractor pull. (ABC News: Lua Ikenasio)

Mr McKenzie initially joined a Vintage Machinery Society with his own father before becoming a TRACS member two decades ago.

He is now a collector and is "pleased" Angus is taking an interest.

"I try and take a bit of credit for it," Mr McKenzie said.

"But ever since he was a little fella, he's always been around our shed, playing around with things and trying to fix things up."

Now, with six years of driving experience and two tractor pulls under his belt, Angus knows his way around the machines.

After helping his grandfather rebuild the tractor he competed in last year, he is now working on a couple of his own projects.

Angus McKenzie stands on the sideline as his grandfather competes in the tractor pull (ABC News: Lua Ikenasio)

The future of tractor pulling

The generational connection is becoming increasingly important for the TRACS club.

While it boasts 130 members, many are aged in their 70s and 80s.

Mr McKenzie said attracting young people to the club was critical.

"When we all fizzle out, who's going to be left if the young ones don't come along?" he said.

"So it's good to see a few young ones starting to come through the system and get a bit of an interest now, and then hopefully they can carry it on when we fade away."

Mr Kovac agreed, saying the club needed to encourage more children to get involved so the sport could continue into the future.

For now, the youngest members are learning from the people who came before them.

title: 'Economically disastrous': One Nation's early access super scheme slammed
text:
Barnaby Joyce has insisted inflation caused by One Nation's proposed superannuation early access scheme would be "undetectable", despite warnings it would create a sugar hit for Australians while making the cost-of-living crisis worse in the long term.

Under the proposal, Australians with a mortgage or paying rent would be given a choice to divert a portion of their superannuation to their take-home pay for up to three years under a One Nation proposal.

The full 12 per cent compulsory super contribution would still be paid by employers, but 3 per cent would be paid directly to the person by the super fund if they opted in.

The payments would also remain subject to the concessional tax rate of 15 per cent, rather than the higher personal income tax rate.

Are the super wars another Mediscare? A political war over superannuation has been inflamed in the past fortnight.

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson said the average full-time worker earning about $90,500 would get an extra $2,300 in their pocket each year.

That works out to about $44 a week, which Senator Hanson said would provide "breathing room".

"For a working couple earning $168,000 between them, it is about $4,300 a year after tax, or $82 a week, back in the family budget," she said.

The senator said anyone would be allowed to apply to alleviate cost of living pressures, because it was "their money".

Judo Bank chief economic advisor Warren Hogan said the proposal would provide short-term relief for Australians but raise the cost of living over the long-term.

"There is no example in recorded history of us effectively getting our cost-of-living issues under control with more spending," he said.

"It ultimately makes the problem worse. We need to bring demand in the economy down to take pressure of the supply side in our economy to allow price pressures to ease."

The Reserve Bank has increased interest rates three consecutive times this year in an attempt to curb inflation.

Mr Hogan said under the guardrails set out in the policy, almost two-thirds of adult Australians would be eligible.

"An initiative like this will put money in people's pockets at an average of 50 or 60 bucks a week, and that money multiplied over half the population, probably, will be a significant stimulus and make the inflation problem worse," he said.

But Mr Joyce insisted the inflationary impact would be "incredibly small".

"If the money is going to your house payments it's still the same," he said.

Industry peak body Association of Superannuation Funds of Australia (ASFA) labelled the proposal "economically disastrous" and said it would push up inflation while making people poorer in retirement.

"This proposal would not alleviate the cost of living. It would drive the cost of living higher," CEO Mary Delahunty said.

"Allowing people to take out three per cent is the thin end of the wedge that could erode one of the greatest policy success stories this country has."

One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce has insisted the policy would not increase inflation. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Plan would erode retirement nest egg

Health Minister Mark Butler labelled the proposal an "absolutely terrible plan" and pointed to the Morrison government's experiment allowing people to access more of their super during the COVID-19 pandemic, which left some with a depleted nest egg.

"It's going to make a huge difference, a bad difference to their retirement decades down the track," he said.

Analysis from the Super Members Council showed a typical 30-year-old full-time worker who withdraws superannuation under the early access policy for three years would be about $25,000 worse off at retirement.

Can you access your super savings before retirement? Should you tap into your super early? There is a trade-off between instant cash and future growth.

Over the full three years, that person would get about $6,900 in their pocket but miss out on more than $18,000 in compounding interest by retirement.

But Senator Hanson said she would prefer Australians to access their super early if they were "on the cusp of losing their home" or "out on the street".

"I would rather see them get that help and assistance they need now, not later in life," she said.

Australians are already allowed to access their superannuation before retirement for several reasons, including financial or medical hardship.

Deputy Liberal leader Jane Hume dismissed the proposal as nothing more than a "headline" and said One Nation had questions to answer about how the policy would interact with a person's super balance or their concessional caps.

"This so far is nothing more than a headline. It hasn't really been explained," she said.

" Are we turning our superannuation funds into banks? "

Nationals MP David Littleproud said there was a serious risk of "unintended consequences" of the proposal, including the potential for higher inflation.

"When you've got inflation out of control at the moment, and you fuel that with putting more money into the economy, the unintended consequence is that inflation will go up and interest rates will go up," he said.

One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce defended the policy and claimed the current system for early access, where the person must prove they are experiencing hardship, was "incredibly convoluted".

Asked whether One Nation should spell out to people that taking money out of their super now would affect their balance in the future, Mr Joyce said, "people are competent enough to work that out for themselves".

"People aren't stupid," he said.

"There's no point telling a family they'll be better off in retirement if they can't afford the mortgage or their rent payment today," he said.

" A good retirement starts with keeping a roof over your head. "

Minister for Social Services Tanya Plibersek said One Nation was attempting to "raid" Australians' super instead of facilitating a real pay increase.

She said people who opted in to the plan would be "thousands of dollars worse off in retirement".

title: Mary Fowler kicks off Manchester City season with opening goal
text:
Matildas star Mary Fowler has kicked off her 2026/27 Women's Super League season by scoring Manchester City's opening goal in a 3-1 win over Birmingham City.

Bunny Shaw was player of the match for her double, but Fowler started the day with a brilliant first-time strike to set the tone for the reigning champions.

After a goalless first half, Fowler worked down the right wing, where her cross was deflected and Neve Herron's hack ended at the feet of Laura Blindkilde Brown.

She then tried a second cross and, after another failed clearance by Geum-min Lee, the ball returned to Fowler, who fired a first-time strike into the bottom right corner.

Her 49th-minute goal was quickly followed by Shaw's first, nodding home a well-directed corner from Kerstin Casparij.

Shaw, last season's leading scorer and Professional Footballers' Association player of the year, repeated the feat in the shadows of full-time before newly promoted Birmingham got a consolation goal through Oceane Hurtre in the 90th minute.

Crystal Palace, who finished second behind Birmingham in WSL 2 last season, enjoyed a happier return to the ‌top ​division, beating Everton ⁠1-0 through Lexi Lloyd-Smith's 34th-minute winner.

Last season's runners-up Arsenal secured a 1-0 win at Brighton & Hove Albion earlier on Sunday, with 19-year-old winger Lisa Baum marking her club debut by surging forward ⁠from midfield and finishing left-footed from a tight angle in the 10th minute.

title: Spinning mill blueprint could provide path to manufacturing revival
text:
Australia's chief science agency has created a blueprint to re-establish spinning mills, a vital link in the country's clothing supply chain that disappeared in the 1980s.

The CSIRO report looked at the feasibility of spinning mills, producing a template manufacturers can use to re-establish domestic production.

While small parts of the textile and clothing sector have survived the offshoring trend of the past four decades, this critical link from farm to hanger is completely missing.

As changes to global trade and technology make the return of spinning possible, the fashion industry is warning it will take significant investment to make it probable.

To encourage it, they are calling on the nation's largest purchaser of uniforms to guarantee demand by committing to Australian-made.

Raw fibre or synthetics can be spun into yarn to make textiles or thread. (Supplied: Stu Ross, Milk Video)

Spinning yarn

A spinning mill is a factory where raw cotton, wool or synthetic fibres like polyester are twisted together, or spun, to make yarn and thread that can be woven into textiles.

Facing worker shortages, rising electricity costs and cheap garments made overseas, spinning mills have disappeared from Australia over the past 40 years.

Australian Fashion Council (AFC) chief executive Sam Delgos said the industry saw value in producing the material and end garment solely in the country.

"Textile, clothing and footwear manufacturing contracted sharply in the 1980s after the import tariffs were removed," she said.

Sam Delgos says the industry wants Australia to have capability at every stage of the manufacturing process. (Supplied: Australian Fashion Council)

Earlier this year, AFC released its own national manufacturing strategy to bring it back.

"The industry is very clear they want the capability to be able to take our Australian-grown cotton and wool all the way from farm to finished garment here," Ms Delgos said.

"Every stage of that process that we're not doing in Australia is values, jobs and of course traceability of our supply chain that we're handing over to another country."

Australia sends raw cotton overseas to countries like China to be spun into yarn and thread. (ABC News: Brett Worthington)

Template for return

The CSIRO study was funded by the cotton industry and the federal government through Cotton Research and Development Corporation (CRDC).

The study's author, senior principal research scientist Stuart Gordon, said the work could be used by companies exploring establishing a mill as a blueprint and scaled to their specific needs.

"It provides a reasonably objective template for people to run a more focused business case," Dr Gordon said.

Stuart Gordon says the blueprint can be scaled to a company's needs. (Supplied: CSIRO)

The study considered challenges like the cost of electricity and workforce skill shortages, as well as where mills could be built. It identified Toowoomba and Brisbane in Queensland, Narrabri, Dubbo and Sydney in New South Wales and Melbourne in Victoria as potential locations.

Dr Gordon said it allowed companies to compare being closer to the inputs, like cotton or wool growing regions, or closer to textile manufacturers and ports where the yarn will be exported.

"If we have it in Toowoomba, the cost to the mill there is quite low, but the cost of the goods out of the mill, to the local manufacturers at least, is quite high," he said.

'A unique capability'

The study specifically looked at the feasibility of short-staple spinning, a technique primarily used for cotton.

Peak industry body Cotton Australia chief executive Adam Kay said advances in technology had mitigated some of the issues that had led production to move overseas.

"Spinning mills, they're all automated, there's very little labour [now]," he said.

"The key thing is apparently the energy costs to run the mill.

"If energy costs can come down, that will make it attractive to have spinning back in Australia [which is] certainly, something we'd love to see."

This shows the different fibre lengths of wool and cotton. (Supplied: Eqwools)

The short-staple spinning system can also take other fibres like synthetics, recycled fibres, hemp and even a special type of wool.

Wool is traditionally spun in a long-staple mill, but Australian company Michell Wool has figured out how to spin the shorter part of the wool clip in the system.

General manager Gaynor Scott said the company had no choice but to send the shorter wool overseas to be spun.

She wanted to see spinning return to Australia.

"That would give us a really unique capability," she said.

Alongside being able to supply the domestic industry, Ms Scott said it would open up opportunities to export yarn to international textile manufacturers.

"It would also be really important to have that manufacturing capability from a providence standpoint," she said.

Wool and cotton spinning is the only step of textile manufacturing that is not available in Australia. (Supplied: Eqwools)

Guaranteed demand

While the AFC welcomed the feasibility study, Ms Delgos said manufacturers needed confidence in ongoing demand before they invested.

That could be achieved by getting the largest purchasers of clothing and textiles in the country to buy Australian-made.

"The government procurement of uniforms, defence apparel, would be one of the few levers that can create certainty at scale," she said.

"At the moment, we actually don't have any verifiable information about what percentage of contracts were actually landing with Australian manufacturers."

Exciting Australian textile experiment Scientists, farmers and the fashion industry collaborate to create a natural fabric made from a blend of wool and cotton.

Each department in the federal government runs its own procurement, but the policy they adhere to sits under the finance department.

A spokesperson for the department said there was a range of measures to promote domestic economic growth through procurement.

It said that included targets to source from small to medium enterprises and requirements to first consider Australian businesses and the benefit to the economy.

"The government continues to engage with industry and stakeholders to ensure the commonwealth procurement framework supports competitive Australian businesses while maintaining value for money and open, transparent procurement processes," they said.

title: Forehand rocket shows Carlos Alcaraz back to 'full power' in US Open win
text:
Carlos Alcaraz has beaten American 20th seed Tommy Paul 6-4, 6-3, 6-4 to reach the quarterfinals of the US Open and remain ​firmly on track for back-to-back titles at Flushing Meadows.

The seven-time grand slam champion has hit top form in New York after nearly five months out with a right wrist injury and extended his major match-winning streak to 18 with a stunning display of shot-making.

It included a blistering 164km/h forehand winner down the line as he established an advantage early in the second set on Arthur Ashe Stadium.

For a man who missed the past two slams and has been out since April due to a wrist injury, an ailment that had ended or stunted multiple tennis careers, it was an indicator that he is back to "full power".

It was one of 33 winners for Alcaraz, including another rocket of a forehand to bring up match point at a venue where he has thrived ever since his maiden major triumph four years ago.

"I think so," ⁠Alcaraz said when asked about being back to his best in New York, where he has reached the quarterfinals in five of his six ‌appearances now.

"It shows ‌how special this place is to me. I'm just trying to enjoy my time on the court, so it probably doesn't matter that I was out for four and a half months.

"Every time I come here, I play my best."

Despite the scoreline, Alcaraz was pushed by the speed demon on the other side of the net, with Paul pulling out his second around-the-post winner of the tournament.

The Spaniard was unfazed.

"I think I ‌just played my game," Alcaraz said.

"I tried to play to my style. Tommy's such a talented player and his shots are pretty dangerous and it's difficult to ‌control the ball when it comes to you. I was ready for a battle.

"I was trying to ⁠be aggressive all the time … I did well to put pressure on his ‌return, which helped me stay calm and to ​think clearly. I was really ‌happy with the performance."

Even with much of the showcourt crowd yearning for ‌a home winner, second seed Alcaraz ‌continued to steal the show with his audacious play and moved to the brink of improving his win-loss record against ‌American players at the grand slams to 13-0.

After shifting down to cruise mode, Alcaraz briefly flinched at the finish line, but he regrouped to deliver the knockout blow and set ‌up a ​meeting with American Ben Shelton, who swept aside Greece's Stefanos Tsitsipas 6-2, 6-3, 6-4.

On the other side of the draw, Frances Tiafoe beat Daniil Medvedev 7-6(7/1), 6-4, 7-6(8/6) to set up an all-American quarterfinal with Alex Michelsen.

The 22-year-old beat 27th-seeded Argentinian Tomas Martin Etcheverry 7-6(8/6), 6-4, 6-4 in their fourth-round clash.

title: Elder among last to remember Australia's forgotten 'parkland'
text:
Menang Elder Aunty Carol Petterson was four years old when her family worked as shepherds.

They would drive the herd through bushland and along rivers towards the West Australian coast.

Standing on the same rocks they once used to cross the Gairdner River, about 200 kilometres south-east of Perth, she has vivid memories of the landscape.

The station employed both white and Aboriginal station hands. (ABC Great Southern: Astrid Volzke)

"There were no fences around … it was like a parkland," she said.

"I can still visualise it."

This Place - ABC Education From the name of a town or street, a mountain or creek, place names are starting point for learning more about Australia's first languages and cultures.

The family didn't have dogs; they drove the sheep themselves, and so long as the lead sheep was headed in the right direction, the rest would follow.

"I had a wonderful childhood," she said.

"We didn't have motor cars, and I almost feel like I'm from the dinosaur era because we walked."

And walk they did, managing up to 20 kilometres a day, keeping pace with the horse and cart carrying their gear.

The once-abundant "parkland" is now a productive farming region. (ABC Great Southern: Mark Bennett)

Back then, places were known only by their Noongar names.

Nearby Jerramungup was Yarramoup, "up" meaning "place" of the "tall" (yarra), "yate" trees (mo).

Aunty Carol said it was the only place around where yate trees grew on a hill.

"So when the people said Yarramoup, you knew where to go because we'd follow the hills and the landmarks to know where we were going," she said.

Ethel Hassell recorded her observations of station life in her 19th-century book My Dusky Friends, which included a map of Aboriginal "tribes". (ABC Great Southern: Astrid Volzke)

They learned to read the country around them.

"We knew about the weather, we knew about the animals, we knew where the bush foods were," she said.

"If there was samphire by the creek, we would wrap it up in paperbark with meat and put it on the coals.

"We gathered our salt from the bush and our sweetness from honey.

"To this day, I don't use sugar, and very little salt."

Aunty Carol says the bush had everything they needed, like this salty samphire. (ABC Great Southern: Astrid Volzke)

For Aunty Carol, country provided everything they needed.

"It's home," she said.

"When you look at the bush, it's our kitchen, it's our dining room, it's our yarning room, it's our classroom, it's our study area, it's our therapeutic area."

But the country Aunty Carol remembers was a much richer and more abundant landscape than the one seen today.

For Aunty Carol, the bush was the kitchen, dining room, yarning room and classroom. (ABC Great Southern: Astrid Volzke)

Gondwana Link chief executive Keith Bradby has studied early explorer journals to understand just how dramatically the landscape and its wildlife have changed.

"I've read the early explorer journals, trying to understand how different the country was then, because there's no question it was very different," he said.

"You had people like James Drummond, who went through that country in the 1840s, just marvelling at its botanical richness.

"If you read the early journals, the big hazard of riding through the bush was that woylies and tammars would just bolt out all the time and startle the horses."

Keith Bradby says the conservation program aims to restore a 1,000-kilometre stretch of bushland in WA's south. (ABC Great Southern: Astrid Volzke)

An excerpt from surveyor John Septimus Roe's journal, dated October 22, 1848, described it as "a large extent of good grassy country … well watered by a river and its numerous branches".

But by 1950, the Hassell Estate was sold to the state government and mass clearing began to make way for post-war soldier resettlement.

Aunty Carol and her siblings are among the last to remember what it was like before that time.

Aunty Carol's parents worked for the Hassell family, whose estate covered 20,000 acres. (ABC Great Southern: Mark Bennett)

She hopes her story will inspire people to reconnect with country.

"We don't see any separation, everything is whole," she said.

"Everything is connected, and we are only just one little part of that."

In a savvy move that will see it vault from explorer to producer, Aureka Limited has tabled a binding agreement to acquire a producing Victorian gold mine and a strategically vital processing mill in a low-cash, scrip-heavy deal. The transaction lands squarely in the middle of a renewed wave of mergers and acquisitions in the Australian gold sector, where the market is tending to reward near-term production and cash flow over long-dated development stories. Under the terms of the deal, the company is set to acquire 100 per cent of High Grade Holdings (HGH), the parent company that owns the Fiddlers Creek gold and silver mine, along with 100 per cent of Vanning Resources, the operator of the 42,000-tonne-per-annum Wedderburn gold processing mill, for a base consideration of $8.9 million. Aureka Limited’s acquisition includes the operating 42,000-tonne-per-annum Wedderburn gold processing mill near its other gold projects in Victoria. The dual purchase has been structured as a majority-scrip transaction, comprising just $2.5 million in cash and $6.4 million in Aureka shares issued at 12 cents a pop. Aureka will also reimburse $500,000 in rehabilitation bonds. To fund the play, the company has locked in commitments for a two-tranche placement to raise A$5.65 million, which it says was supported by its significant shareholders. A matching share purchase plan to raise $1.5 million will also be offered to existing shareholders. The centrepiece of the deal is the Wedderburn processing mill, one of only six licensed gold mills in Victoria. With operating infrastructure relatively scarce in the state, control of a plant with stated spare capacity and a licence for external tolling could prove a strategic coup.

‘A low-cash majority scrip transaction at a compelling price-this is a transformative deal for Aureka.’ Aureka Limited managing director James Gurry The mill currently processes high-grade ore from the Fiddlers Creek underground mine, which restarted production in 2025. Aureka due diligence showed HGH has been generating positive monthly free cash flow since the second quarter of this year, just nine months after first production. During its fiscal 2026 ramp-up, the operation churned out 416 ounces of gold from ore with an impressive average head grade of seven grams per tonne (g/t). Recoveries averaged 86 per cent and hit a high of 91 per cent, producing a concentrate with a gold grade of about 70g/t, which is then sold under an existing offtake agreement. Notably, the deal also includes significant exploration upside on the acquired ground. The Fiddlers Creek mine lies within the Percydale goldfield, which has a history of producing over 700,000 ounces of gold. The surrounding tenure contains six kilometres of mineralised structure and more than 600 historical workings, with multiple parallel quartz-reef zones that have never seen a drill bit. As part of the deal, Aureka has committed to drilling at least 1800 metres on the acquired ground. Notably, the ASX has confirmed that Aureka will not need to re-comply with listing rules. HGH will have the right to nominate one non-executive director to Aureka’s board to ensure continuity. Up to a further $2 million in performance payments could be payable over three years if key milestones are hit. These are tied to cumulative production hurdles of 900 ounces of gold within 12 months 2500 ounces within two years and 4000 ounces within three years. An additional milestone concerns the delivery of a JORC-compliant resource for Fiddlers Creek, for which Aureka has yet to report an estimate.

Aureka managing director James Gurry said: “This transaction accelerates Aureka’s existing strategy of targeting opportunistic first-up production:Aureka would immediately become a producer, and with its own mill, which unlocks commercial possibilities for all of Aureka’s projects, including the flagship Irvine Gold Project hosting an estimated 398koz of inferred JORC mineral resource.” Aureka says the new assets are a natural fit with its flagship Irvine gold project, which sits just 16 kilometres from the world-class 5-million-ounce Stawell gold mine and already hosts a 398,000-ounce inferred JORC resource. The company is currently drill-testing extensions to Irvine’s 358,000-ounce Resolution Lode and says that, despite 59 kilometres of drilling since 2107, the geological understanding is still in its infancy, leaving plenty of blue sky for further growth. A key advantage of the new deal lies in the proximity of Aureka’s 56,500-ounce Comstock project at St Arnaud, which sits less than 50km from the Wedderburn mill, potentially providing a clear pathway to market for a second production source. The St Arnaud goldfield itself is a well-endowed region, with historical production of 400,000 ounces of gold at a stunning average grade of 15g/t. The company’s wider regional tenement holdings also include the Jubilee gold project near Ballarat and the Morning Bill gold and base metals project. With elevated gold prices improving the economics of smaller-scale operations and restarts, Aureka’s timing looks astute. By snapping up a cash-flowing asset, the company has not just bought a mine, but a strategic platform to help self-fund larger-scale exploration at its flagship Irvine play.

Billionaire mining and media scion Ryan Stokes is the new chairman of the company that owns the Seven Network along with The West Australian and Triple M, becoming the fourth person to hold the role since the corporation was created via a merger at the beginning of the year. Stokes’ father, Kerry, stepped down as chairman of the company in February after engineering the merger of his TV and newspaper empire, Seven West Media, with radio company Southern Cross Austereo. Ryan Stokes is the new chair of the company that controls Seven, The West Australian, and numerous radio stations. Brent Lewin It has been a tumultuous start for the merged company. A number of executives from the Seven side of the business were ousted before the Stokes family took back control in a series of moves culminating in Monday’s announcement that Ryan Stokes would succeed Teresa Dyson, a longtime family associate, as company chair. The longtime controlling shareholders of Seven had their control of the company halved in the deal. Two weeks ago, the Stokes family bought back into the company for the first time since the transaction, with their Seven Group Holdings entity – which also owns mining equipment company WestTrac and machinery hire firm Coates – upping its stake in Southern Cross from 20.2 per cent to 23.2 per cent.

Advertisement

Ryan Stokes is also chief executive of Seven Group, and while he has been a director representing the group’s shareholding for some time, it is widely known that he does not share the same love for the family’s media assets as his father. Alongside the Seven Network, the company wields significant influence in WA through West Australian Newspapers, located where the Stokes’ mining business largely operates. The company also owns the Triple M and Hit radio networks, and the LiSTNR digital audio platform. Less than a year ago, the companies announced the deal which would result in Kerry Stokes retiring, Southern Cross chair Heith Mackay-Cruise taking over as chair of the combined company, and Seven boss Jeff Howard stepping in as chief executive. All three have since left the company’s management team and board, and the company is expected to formally rename itself under the Seven banner in the coming months. As part of that deal, and by ceding control of Seven, the Stokes family reportedly extracted about $180 million in tax benefits based on the losses it accrued over the course of the family’s ownership. But just over six months later, the family has re-emerged as the power behind the board, and in another six months, they could effectively control it by taking their shareholding beyond 25 per cent. Dyson will remain on the board as an independent director, but there was no room in Monday’s announcement for former Stokes lieutenant Bruce McWilliam, who has emerged as a major shareholder with the financial backing of another Perth-based billionaire, Gina Rinehart.

Cathy O’Connor, who led Lachlan Murdoch’s Nova Entertainment radio company for almost 20 years, and was recently chief executive of outdoor media company oOh!media, was also elected as lead independent director. She said the board had established her role, a majority of independent directors, and independent directors of its committees to ensure good governance.

title: It’s gambling dressed up as trading, and it’s taken over the US Open
text:
Advertisement

SportTennisUS Open It’s gambling dressed up as trading, and it’s taken over the US Open Michael Koziol September 7, 2026 — 12:58pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

New York: Logan Gornbein is very clear: his presence at the US Open is dependent on his ability to gamble. “I would not be here if I did not have my Kalshi account,” the 23-year-old New Yorker says, naming the booming prediction market company that has just inked a multi-year deal with the US Tennis Association. Logan Gorbein (left) and Adam Meitus, both 23, at the US Open. They use prediction markets to gamble on tennis while at the tournament. Michael Koziol “I just love being able to watch live and watch my prediction. It makes it a lot more fun. I think that prediction markets are the future. If I was able to invest in a prediction market, I would.” Sports betting has become increasingly popular in the US since the Supreme Court struck down a federal ban in 2018.

Advertisement

This is the reality of a major sporting event in 2026: betting is not some kind of tangent or afterthought. It is integral to the experience for many fans. In the stands, plenty of people – young men, mostly – can be seen flicking through Kalshi or Polymarket, the other major US prediction market, monitoring trades and stats. These platforms are now worth tens of billions of dollars and are growing exponentially. So far, they are not licensed to operate in Australia – in the case of Polymarket, it has been explicitly banned by the Australian Communications and Media Authority. Prediction markets offer odds on future events: the results of sporting matches, whether or when something will occur, what Donald Trump will say in a speech. People buy contracts in the outcome, and the price – or perceived likelihood of something happening – is set by the market. The companies dress this up as a financial product, but it is effectively just wagering. Live betting is allowed, and it’s where the action happens. USTA chief executive Craig Tiley, who ran the Australian Open for two decades until he left earlier this year. Getty Images If that is the future, the future is already here in New York. As the tournament began, new USTA chief executive Craig Tiley, formerly the long-time boss of Tennis Australia and tournament director of the Australian Open, announced a multi-year partnership making Kalshi the official prediction market of the US Open.

Advertisement

“We’re relentless about keeping tennis at the cutting edge of global sports innovation and fan connection,” he said. “Partnering with Kalshi gives us an opportunity to pioneer that next generation of fan engagement while ensuring the integrity of our sport.” Kalshi chief executive Tarek Mansour said tennis was one of the fastest growing sports on the platform. In August, Polymarket became the official prediction market partner for the ATP, the body that runs the men’s tennis tour, covering about 20,000 matches per season. The deal includes exclusive streaming rights, meaning Polymarket users can watch matches live through that platform, along with real-time data, side-by-side with betting options (or “opportunities to trade”). In any given stadium at the US Open, a healthy number of fans will be monitoring the match through a prediction market. Getty Images Polymarket’s head of sports business development, Ari Borod, noted tennis was a “natural fit” for prediction markets because of how momentum shifted point-by-point. That created “opportunities for expectations to change in real time”.

Advertisement

Related Article US Open Why this week could bring an end to the great American tennis chase And prediction markets enable real-time wagering on highly specific outcomes: who wins a set, the exact match score, total number of games, you name it. The US Open has even started sending push notifications to people’s phones about match predictions, “presented by Kalshi”. On the grounds, it was not difficult to find prediction market enthusiasts in the throng. Outside centre court, a man was walking around with a Kalshi microphone and camera, interviewing punters. Among every group of young men that this masthead approached, at least one – typically most – were avid sports gamblers. “It’s fantastic, absolutely fantastic,” said Jordan Levy, a 26-year-old New Yorker, who prefers the sports betting website DraftKings. “Tennis is honestly my favourite sport to bet on. You’re only betting on one guy … to me, you have a better chance of winning.”

Advertisement

Levy says he is up a few thousand dollars since the tournament began. He and his friend Josh Russ have bets on as we speak – for Jiri Lehecka to beat Stefanos Tsitsipas, and for Ben Shelton to prevail over Denis Shapovalov (Lehecka lost, but Shelton won). Just because someone is betting does not mean they are gambling away their entire savings. Gornbein, who said he wouldn’t be here unless he could play the prediction markets, says he is down about $US12.50 (about $17.30). His friend Adam Meitus, also 23, says he has lost $5 – although he struggles to name the player he was just betting on. Josh Russ (left) and Jordan Levy at the US Open. They use sports betting websites and prediction markets such as Kalshi and DraftKings while at the tournament. Michael Koziol But overall, the amount of money at stake is considerable, especially as prediction markets are still relatively new, even in the US. Kalshi’s website shows just over $US11 million (about $15.3 million) was traded on the Lehecka-Tsitsipas match by the time it ended. As it entered a fifth set on Saturday, a match between Taylor Fritz and Francisco Cerundolo had eclipsed $US8 million ($11.1 million). People have already wagered $US21 million (almost $30 million) on the tournament’s eventual winner. Most people bet responsibly and say it adds to their enjoyment of the experience. Obviously, the dangers of gambling addiction are well known. But there can also be impacts on the players from gamblers who turn ugly when things don’t go their way.

Advertisement

American world No. 3 Jessica Pegula said during a post-match press conference that it was a tricky matter. The International Tennis Integrity prohibits players from entering any sponsorship deals with betting companies. Tournaments have no such qualms. “We get a lot of negativity from people that use stuff like that, bettors – whether you win or lose, it doesn’t even matter sometimes. We get a lot of hate for it on social media,” Pegula said. “So, it’s tough when you see that and they’re a big sponsor behind the court, or they’re on TV. American world No.3 Jessica Pegula said prediction markets were inevitable, but she was uneasy about official partnerships. Getty Images “I don’t really know the best way to deal with it, just because it’s kind of the inevitable. It’s everywhere, it’s not really going away any time soon – especially when I look at other sports. Betting is a big part of keeping fans engaged. I go back and forth with that one.” Other players, or former players, are leaning in. Five-time grand slam winner Maria Sharapova, who retired in 2020, is fronting an advertising campaign for Polymarket.

title: More than 200 staff stood down at collapsed developer Bathla
text:
Advertisement

More than 200 staff have been stood down from the collapsed Bathla Group after a weekend of crisis talks, as administrators confirmed construction on developments in Sydney would be suspended. Bathla said in a statement on Monday that it had reached a short-term funding agreement with five lenders to enable limited operations to continue for a further two weeks, but 213 staff had been stood down and “construction on other projects will be suspended today”. Drivers bring vehicles into Bathla’s Girraween headquarters for what appears to be an odometer reading as staff are informed of the latest developments. Janie Barrett The developer, which has major projects across Sydney and thousands of properties in the pipeline, collapsed into voluntary administration on August 24 owing dozens of creditors $3.4 billion and has been teetering on the brink of liquidation. Teneo senior managing director Stephen Longley, the administrator, said on Monday the immediate priority had been securing enough short-term funding “to maintain a minimum viable operating structure”.

Advertisement

“The arrangements agreed today allow us to provide the central support required for construction to continue on projects associated with the lenders participating in the funding package,” he said. “Significant work remains to secure the funding required to progress and ultimately complete all projects currently under construction. We will continue to work closely with lenders and other key stakeholders to pursue those arrangements.” More than 200 Bathla employees have been stood down. Janie Barrett The administrators said that final documentation was expected to be signed later on Monday but the amount and the participating lenders would remain confidential. Further updates were expected to be provided to customers, employees, creditors, subcontractors and other stakeholders as the administration progressed. Premier Chris Minns said on Monday that the state government was “in discussions with the administrator” and noted while payroll was met last week “we’ve got a bit of a way to run”.

Advertisement

“There is still prospect for either the breaking up of the company and other parties stepping in to grab a piece of it and complete the works,” Minns said. “So I think that there’s an important process to take place before a line of credit or public money is extended to the company. And the reason today is it’s not my money; it’s public money.” Bathla’s headquarters in Girraween, which appeared quiet after the announcement. Janie Barrett Minns said it was possible for third parties to take over parts of the company: “In which case, the administration process will work for those home owners.” “Not all major builders in NSW are financed the same way. You know, this is a very strange corporate structure involving a hell of a lot of debt, largely collected from private capital, private credit, not through the banks and traditional finances,” he said.

Advertisement

Opposition Leader Kellie Sloane said she felt for those who had lost their jobs and was concerned for the companies and subcontractors who were owed money. “You know this collapse isn’t just one company; it’s affecting so many people and so many potential home owners as well, up to a couple of thousand of them.” Related Article Exclusive

Bathla collapse Developer Bathla told to fix defects as it staves off liquidation One Bathla employee leaving the company’s Girraween headquarters on Monday said he had not been stood down, but other staff had been. He did not confirm how many employees no longer have work and said he remained “positive” about Bathla’s future. After the announcement, Bathla’s headquarters remained quiet, with the few staff spotted leaving the site keeping their heads down and declining to speak to this masthead.

Advertisement

Outside the building, the car park was full with every kind of vehicle, from utes to BMWs. About five people could be seen through the glass windows, typing on their laptop. The group’s director, Bhart Bhushan, was not seen at the building. One person leaving the building said they were not a Bathla employee but had been brought in to “fix stuff” before another company could take the headquarters over. Bathla is leasing the Girraween site. Related Article Property development He was the ‘Baron of Blacktown’ – then his empire fell apart On Friday, it was revealed that Bathla Group owed at least $3.4 billion and administrator Teneo told creditors that “positive discussions” were continuing with five of the company’s 43 lenders to gain funding to keep construction going. Bathla Group – and its 542 individual entities – entered into voluntary administration on August 24. Teneo was last week desperately negotiating with lenders to secure short-term funding to stave off liquidation.

Advertisement

Bathla has 45 projects under construction in NSW set to deliver about 2500 homes, but administrators said the developer also has a significant land bank holding, at various stages of development. The administrator is also seeking to prevent the suspension of Bathla Group’s building licences by Building Commission NSW, which issued the notice of intention after the company entered voluntary administration. If the developer goes into liquidation, the licences would be automatically cancelled. Later on Friday, the state’s building regulator hit Raj & Jai Construction, a related entity of Bathla’s, with a building work rectification order to fix seven serious defects at an apartment building in Seven Hills. title: NRL stars fear set restarts could decide a final. V’landys says they’re ‘not telling the truth’
text:
