SportNRLNRL 2026 NRL stars fear set restarts could decide a final. V’landys says they’re ‘not telling the truth’ Dan Walsh September 7, 2026 — 12:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

ARL Commission chair Peter V’landys says players are “not telling the truth” amid a renewed spate of criticism for the NRL’s expanded set restart rules, with Roosters skipper James Tedesco warning that contentious ruck interpretations could decide a club’s season. Tedesco and Cowboys counterpart Tom Dearden were among the finals captains to most strongly echo Harry Grant’s criticism after Melbourne’s win over Cronulla on Saturday night. Loading That match featured 24 infringements and 26 errors. Grant, the Storm, Maroons and Kangaroos hooker, then said the NRL needs to work out “do we want to play touch football or rugby league?” The governing body’s widened six-again remit – which sees a new set called for ruck infringements or offsides beyond the 20-metre line – has been a talking point all year.

Advertisement

The RLPA has been especially vocal regarding fluctuations in the rules’ enforcement. Data collated by independent statistician The Rugby League Eye Test indicates that set restarts in the final four rounds have increased to an average of 8.4 per game. That is a rise of almost 30 per cent from the 6.5 set restarts averaged per game between rounds 14-23. V’landys came out swinging in response to critiques from the players at the NRL’s finals launch on Monday morning, all but declaring the rules will remain as they are for 2027 despite the game’s long-held policy of reviewing all on-field matters at the end of each season. As Tedesco reiterated the concerns of numerous players, coaches and fans that set-restarts are awarded on the run and ruck infringements are not properly explained by officials, V’landys offered a blunt dismissal. “I don’t buy that,” he said.

Advertisement

“The two six-again [infringements] are 10-metre compliance, and this year we have 98 per cent compliance on the 10-metre [zone]. So it’s proven that if you have a deterrent there on a six-again, players will abide by the rule … And the fans did not like wrestling. The players know when they’re trying to control the ruck speed. James Tedesco is the latest high-profile player to raise concerns over set restart rules. Sitthixay Ditthavong “I think that they’re not telling the truth if they believe (that) when they’re given a six again, they didn’t know what it was for. I mean, I think it’s pretty obvious.” Tedesco said he was less certain than ever on why some set restarts were awarded while he has been out injured and watching Roosters games from the sidelines. “And I understand the referees are working hard, but when I’m on the field it’s hard to get a clarification of why we’re getting pinged at the ruck, so we don’t know what we need to clean up,” he said.

Advertisement

“I understand Peter is very focused on getting the ruck speed right, but personally, there’s a lot of times I’m not sure why a six-again is called. “I don’t really know how we get things more consistent either, but it probably is something we need to be aware of in the final series. You can’t let the games be decided by like six-again or set restarts, but you worry that could happen.” Dearden’s Cowboys side have been involved in as many wild, high-scoring shoot-outs as any side this season, with the Queensland and Australian Test player pointing to the new six-again rules as a key influence. “Personally, I’m old school, and I think we had the balance of the rules right last year,” he said.

Advertisement

“I’m not a fan of changing the rules every year. I don’t really see the need to keep adjusting or making these significant changes; I’d like a bit more stability in the game.” Asked about the potential of set-restarts being reviewed or potentially wound back in response to widespread player feedback, V’landys said: “I always look at raw figures and raw facts. You can’t base things on gut feeling, or you’ve got to base it on the facts. And at the moment, the facts do not support us changing that rule.” Speaking specifically to Grant’s comments that “you don’t know what constitutes a quick play-the-ball or what constitutes a slow play-the-ball”, V’landys said he has the utmost respect for the Storm captain.

Advertisement

“But he’s got this one wrong,” V’landys said. Related Article Analysis

NRL 2026 Bennett the Bunny whisperer: How Wayne has unlocked Souths’ lost boys “I let facts speak for themselves, and when you look at the facts, the ruck speed is still the same as it was last year. “It’s around 3.5 seconds, and it remains that way. And look, some teams try to take advantage of the ruck and slow the ruck down, and at the moment the referees aren’t allowing them to do that. “Some teams try to get the ruck speed up at over 4 seconds, and it doesn’t sound much, but .5 seconds is a lot, and it does slow the game down.

“So we make no apology that we’re going to keep the ruck speed the same for both teams. So no team gets an advantage any more. “And the referees, in my view, have done a terrific job… the raw numbers don’t back up what Harry’s saying.”

Last Friday, Donald Trump threatened to stop all trade with countries that have trade surpluses with the US ... unless the US Federal Reserve Board cuts interest rates. Donald Trump has shown off his erratic character and economic illiteracy once again. High interest rates put the U.S.A. at a very unfair disadvantage, and I won’t allow that to happen,” he wrote.

It’s not at all clear that Trump has the power to do what he is threatening. The US Supreme Court decision in February that he cites and which ruled his “Liberation Day” tariffs were illegal dealt with a particular piece of legislation – the International Emergency Economic Powers Act – and taxing powers, rather than deciding any questions about the authority the president might have under it or other legislation to simply ban trade with another nation. Trump would spark economic chaos if he carried out his threat. Bloomberg The legal status of the replacement tariffs Trump has subsequently announced (based on the questionable grounds of countries not doing enough to combat slave labour) is being challenged in the courts and has yet to be decided. The presidential authority over trade is one delegated, and limited, by Congress. And the power to ban trade with another country is reserved for declared national emergencies. The Trump administration might be accelerating the US economy towards a financial and economic crisis and national emergency, but it’s not there yet.

Advertisement

It would face a national emergency if Trump were to cut trade with the more than 90 countries with which it has a goods and services trade deficit or the more than 130 countries with which it has a goods trade deficit. Related Article Opinion

Donald Trump Trump is an outlaw. And the US system was not built for an outlaw in the Oval Office Maureen Dowd New York Times columnist Last year, the US goods trade deficit (Trump never includes America’s $US340 billion services surplus) was $US1.2 trillion. Given that those countries that have a trade surplus with the US would probably also import products from the US – the value of their exports would be greater than their trade surpluses – the value of all the trade affected by a ban would be considerably higher. What would happen if he stopped all trading with those surplus countries?

Advertisement

The US dollar’s role as the world’s reserve currency and the centrality of its financial markets (particularly its bond market) to the world financial system promotes imports of both goods and capital. It also effectively lowers their cost for US consumers and businesses while making its exports less competitive. Kevin Warsh is chairman of the US Federal Reserve: It is improbable that the central bank which, unlike the administration, is staffed by a raft of people with economic expertise, will pay any heed to Trump’s “threat”. AP The US consumes more than its poor savings rate can finance. It borrows from the rest of the world to complement its savings and help finance investment and consumption, with the dollar’s singular role lowering the cost of those borrowings. The US imports products that it either doesn’t have or can’t make at sufficient scale itself, or where the imported products are cheaper or are of greater quality or consumer appeal than those it can produce domestically. Some of its imports are components in the global supply chains for products or equipment that are largely manufactured or assembled in the US.

Advertisement

Related Article Exclusive

Interest rates ‘Closer to the red line’: The perfect storm keeping economists awake at night If the US were to shut off imports with those countries that have trade surpluses with it, it wouldn’t have the ability to quickly replace them with domestic production. It wouldn’t, for instance, be able to replace its imports of coffee, bananas, cocoa, tomatoes and other foods immediately, if ever, and it doesn’t have the domestic deposits of rare earths, or copper, or even semiconductors to meet its domestic demand. So there would be severe shortages of some products and massive increases in the prices of those products, and others. Manufacturing plants would close, and jobs would disappear because companies would lose access to global supply chains for the raw resources and intermediate products they rely on.

Advertisement

Almost inevitably, there’d be an exodus of capital from US financial markets. There would be a severe spike in the inflation rate – and interest rates – and a cost-of-living crisis that would dwarf the one Americans are now experiencing. Recession, or something far worse, would be inevitable. The impact could be exacerbated if other countries (which would also be adversely affected, but at least would be able to trade with each other) were to retaliate and block US exports. Regardless, a global recession would be likely. In the longer term, it is conceivable that Trump’s bans on trade might generate more US home-shoring of production, but that wouldn’t moderate the near term shock and, in any event, wouldn’t fill in the vacuum left by the ban on goods that the US doesn’t have the resources to produce. It is improbable that the Fed which, unlike the administration, is staffed by a raft of people with economic expertise, will pay any heed to Trump’s “threat”.

Advertisement

Trade is beyond the Fed’s dual mandate of controlling inflation and maximising jobs and, in any case, the central bankers would recognise the level of destruction and self-harm that execution of Trump’s threat would generate. Patriotism, for the Fed’s governors, involves trying to blunt the impact of Trump’s inflation-inducing policies. The US would face a national emergency if Trump were to cut trade with the more than 90 countries with which it has a goods and services trade deficit or the more than 130 countries with which it has a goods trade deficit. They’d also be acutely aware that while they might be able to provide the anchor point for the US yield curve – the federal funds rate – the rates that businesses and consumers actually pay are set by the market and, with the bond vigilantes re-emerging and bond yields spiking, their focus has to be on lowering the inflation rate. Trump’s unhinged Truth Social post is a sign of the increased anxiety within the White House as the midterm elections loom. He might be right to see those higher bond yields as a threat to Republicans and his presidential authority, but threatening a trade ban unless the Fed does as it’s told will only strengthen the Fed’s resolve to protect its independence and make bond investors even more conscious of the erratic character and economic illiteracy of the president and his policies and the risk, albeit remote, that he might actually try to do what he threatens.

title: Homebuyers left in the dark as embattled property developer Bathla confirms major lay-offs
text:
in brief More than 210 of Bathla's 350 staff were stood down at a meeting in Sydney on Monday morning.

Homebuyers who bought off-the-plan have been left in the dark, uncertain when, or if, their properties will be completed.

Property developer Bathla Group has stood down almost two-thirds of its workforce following its entry into voluntary administration earlier this year.

About 213 of Bathla's 350 staff were stood down at a meeting in Sydney on Monday morning, and construction on several projects has halted as the embattled firm clings to life.

Administrators said they had secured short-term funding to keep some of the firm's projects going.

Insolvency adviser Teneo announced it had secured the funding through five lenders linked to the projects, but the amounts and participants were kept confidential.

Administrator Stephen Longley said the funding would enable Bathla Group to maintain limited operations for a further two weeks while longer-term solutions were explored.

"Our immediate priority has been to secure sufficient short-term funding to maintain a minimum viable operating structure," he said.

"The arrangements agreed allow us to provide the central support required for construction to continue on projects associated with the lenders participating in the funding package.

"Significant work remains to secure the funding required to progress and ultimately complete all projects currently under construction. We will continue to work closely with lenders and other key stakeholders to pursue those arrangements."

Figures presented to creditors put Bathla's total debt at $3.4 billion, including $3.08 billion to secured lenders, $130 million to unsecured lenders, $145 million to the tax office and $4 million to employees.

Bathla is one of Sydney's largest residential developers, with 45 projects under construction.

The home developer entered voluntary administration in late August after the NSW government declined to bail it out.

According to the company's website, the group has 20,000 apartments and 7,000 dwellings in its delivery pipeline, comprising a significant share of the NSW government's target of 75,400 new homes a year for five years until 2029.

Founded in NSW in 1997, Bathla is among a long list of Australian home developers that have recently entered voluntary administration or liquidation.

title: Government warns against One Nation plan for Australians to 'raid' their superannuation
text:
IN BRIEF Under a newly proposed One Nation policy, Australians could access their superannuation earlier and more easily.

Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek said it would leave Australians "worse off in retirement".

One Nation has proposed a new plan to make it easier for Australians to access their superannuation.

The party's plan would allow Australians paying rent or a mortgage to divert a portion of their superannuation directly to their wallet for up to three years.

Employers would still pay the 12 per cent compulsory super contribution, but the super fund would pay 3 per cent to customers who opt in to the plan.

These payments would be taxed at the concessional rate of 15 per cent rather than their personal income tax rate.

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson said the policy would give those struggling with the cost of living crisis "breathing room".

"That's a real boost to help you pay the rent or the mortgage," she said.

title: Qantas flight makes priority landing after engine issue sparks panic over New Zealand
text:
in brief Passengers described a terrifying ordeal after flames and loud bangs were seen coming from the left engine of the plane.

The Boeing 737 landed safely in Christchurch, where emergency crews were waiting.

Emergency services were called to the tarmac when a Qantas flight made a priority landing in Christchurch after an engine issue, which one passenger described as "traumatic".

Liza-Jayne Loch was returning home from a business trip to New Zealand when the Qantas flight ran into trouble.

The plane was climbing above the scenic South Island's mountain ranges on Saturday afternoon, bound for Sydney, when a bang shook the cabin.

A passenger seated nearest the left wing soon shouted, "the engine's on fire", Loch recalled, as the cabin lights began to flicker.

Footage recorded by a passenger and shared with AAP shows flames appearing to issue from the plane's left engine in a series of rapid bursts.

"I was sitting on the left-hand side of the plane, and the flames were very, very visible," Loch said.

"There was a lot of screaming at the time."

As the plane continued to gain altitude, Loch tried to comfort herself by recalling that modern jets could land safely on a single engine.

"That's what I kept in my head, that we could actually fly on one engine," she said.

"But the flames kept coming and the noise kept coming."

QF122 suffered a suspected engine issue shortly after taking off from Queenstown on Saturday afternoon, before making a priority landing at Christchurch.

According to Flight Aware, the Boeing 737 landed about 52 minutes after take-off, touching down shortly before 5pm local time.

The cause of the incident has yet to be determined, but Qantas sent two engineers to Christchurch on Sunday to investigate.

Both engines are thought to have remained in operation for the duration of the flight.

Loch said conditions soon stabilised after the initial shock, while cabin staff took pains to comfort passengers.

"The crew were all terribly, terribly calming," Loch said.

'Massive cheers'

Emergency services were waiting on the tarmac when the flight landed, and passengers were allowed to disembark as normal after a short wait.

"There were massive cheers when we landed," Loch said.

A Qantas spokesperson said the plane was believed to have suffered an engine issue and steps would be taken to support affected customers.

"Our pilots are highly trained to manage situations like this and the aircraft landed safely," they said.

"We know this would have been a distressing experience for passengers and will be contacting all customers to provide support."

Affected passengers were put up in a hotel near the Christchurch International Airport before being booked on a complimentary flight to Sydney on Sunday.

While the second flight went off without a hitch, Loch said nerves were still high.

"I cried getting off the plane when we landed in Sydney," Loch said.

"It was quite traumatic."

title: Labor urges Greens, Coalition to pass social media reforms after 'dawdling and delay'
text:
IN BRIEF Labor is urging the Senate to back reforms aimed at strengthening enforcement of the under-16 social media ban.

The government is also set to unveil draft reforms mandating the ability to opt out of social media algorithms.

Labor is urging the Greens and Coalition to pass laws that would strengthen the eSafety Commissioner's powers to gather information from social media companies and increase fines tech giants face for breaches of the teen social media ban.

When Labor introduced the bill in late June, Communications Minister Anika Wells said an eSafety investigation had suggested several major social media companies were exploiting loopholes in the law.

"The commissioner has found these companies adopting a number of dirty tricks to undermine Australia's law that are straight out of the big-tech playbook," Wells said at the time.

"It is clear ... that social media companies are deliberately failing to comply with our laws."

The bill would give the eSafety Commissioner enhanced information-gathering powers that Labor argues are necessary to ensure social media companies take 'reasonable steps' to prevent under-16s from creating or retaining social media accounts, as required under the ban.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

In March-April, the eSafety Commissioner found 81.5 per cent of 10-15-year-olds were still using at least one age-restricted platform, a small decline from the 85.9 per cent it found before the ban came into effect on 10 December 2025.

However, the government has reported that more than five million social media accounts belonging to under-16s have been deleted, deactivated or restricted since the ban came into effect.

Meta — the parent company of Facebook and Instagram — said in mid-August that it had taken down more than 750,000 accounts and said those numbers would "continue to grow".

"We share the Australian government's goal of ensuring young people have safe, age-appropriate experiences online, and we are meeting our obligations under the law," the company added in a statement released at the time.

'Put politics to the side'

In early July, Greens and Coalition senators voted to send Labor's bill to a Senate inquiry, which eight weeks later recommended the reforms be adopted.

Wells said on Sunday that the decision to send the bill to an inquiry was "the kind of dawdling and delay that has enabled social media companies to get away with harming our kids for so long".

"We have to put politics to the side and pass this bill this week, so the eSafety Commissioner can hold social media companies accountable," she said.

READ MORE This toxic online world has an unstoppable pull. That may be about to change

When voting to refer the bill to the inquiry, Liberal Senator Sarah Henderson accused Labor of trying to "ram through" the new powers without proper scrutiny.

"Rather than Anika Wells' mad scramble to fix her broken ban, much more needs to be done to protect children online," she said.

The Greens also said Labor needed to go further.

"We need to urgently regulate algorithms, and make it clear that social media companies are responsible for the extreme harm their platforms perpetrate," the left-wing party said in its additional comments to the inquiry report.

'Digital duty of care' reforms

The regulation of social media algorithms is an issue that will soon come to the fore in Canberra, with Labor set to release details of proposed laws that would force tech giants to give users the ability to opt out of algorithms.

An exposure draft of the so-called 'digital duty of care' reforms is expected to be released in the coming sitting fortnight.

It would put the onus on social media companies to mitigate risk on their platforms, including actively removing illegal or harmful content.

The option to opt out of algorithms would be mandatory, giving users the choice to take their social media feeds back to the friends-only content they once were.

READ MORE The 'harmful' online rabbit hole finding teens within minutes

Several areas are expected to be identified as off-limits to minors due to the potential for psychological harm, including content that promoted harmful body image.

The changes would prevent boys from being bombarded with violent and misogynistic material, Labor's Matt Thistlethwaite told News24's Sunday Agenda program.

"Many Australian parents have said that they're concerned about their children being exposed to this material," he said.

"We think that the platforms have a responsibility to try and keep young Australian kids safe.

Greens call for larger fines

However, the measures could struggle to pass the Senate in their current form, with Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young saying proposed fines of up to $100 million for breaching the laws were insufficient.

Hanson-Young told reporters that tech companies would see such fines as part of the cost of doing business, and called for penalties to be calculated based on each firm's global profits.

"The power of big tech is so immense and you can't take them on and hit them at their business model with half-baked measures," she said.

READ MORE A landmark US deal could change social media forever

"The government's really going to have to toughen up.

"Either take on big tech properly, or you'll end up putting in place a scheme that really does bugger all."

The Greens are awaiting details of the exposure draft before deciding how to vote, while Senator Hanson-Young has proposed her own bill, calling for an algorithm opt-out to be the default setting.

That measure has been the focus of a campaign by Teach Us Consent's Fix Our Feeds, which has been pushing for linear social media feeds to be the default option.

In a linear social media feed, content would appear in chronological order, with users only seeing posts from people or accounts they have chosen to follow.

The organisation's founder, Chanel Contos, recently said an algorithm opt-out was a good first step, but the measure did not go far enough to stop boys and young men being exposed to harmful content.

"It would fundamentally make the transition onto social media for 16-year-olds and other children safer, and it would bring the principle of affirmative consent to our screens," she told the National Press Club in early September.

Coalition says govt should focus on fixing ban

The Opposition is also yet to establish its position on the proposal, but leader Angus Taylor on Sunday expressed doubts about Labor's plan.

He said parents should have more control over what their children could see on social media, but he was "deeply sceptical" that the proposal wasn't an attempt to censor people's feeds.

Taylor accused Labor of butchering the already implemented under-16s social media ban, which the Coalition supported, adding the government should focus on fixing that policy.

"The government should be focused on that because it's not working," he said.

"So then going off and starting on some other thing ... there's good reason to be sceptical about that."

title: 'Titan of Australian sport': Boxer Tony Mundine honoured at heartfelt Redfern memorial
text:
IN BRIEF Australian boxing great, Tony Mundine, passed away on 30 August from a heart attack.

Mundine remains the only Australian boxer to hold national titles in four weight divisions.

WARNING: This article contains the name and image of an Aboriginal person who has passed away.

Respected Bundjalung boxer Anthony 'Tony' Mundine OAM has been remembered as an "unwavering anchor" of strength and determination at an emotional ceremony in Sydney's Redfern.

Crowds gathered at Redfern Oval on Saturday morning to pay their respects to Mundine, who died from a heart attack on 30 August — aged 75.

His coffin was carried to a small stage — decorated with a large bouquet and the Aboriginal flag proudly draped across the top.

On the side, the dark wood was printed with a pair of boxing gloves and a gold rabbit, a nod to Mundine's loyal, lifelong love of the South Sydney Rabbitohs.

Bundjalung and Gadigal man Craig Madden, nephew to "Uncle Tony", welcomed guests to Country.

He recalled the life of a man who, at 15, came to Sydney to chase his dreams "into the ring".

Madden described Mundine as the "backbone" of their family.

"Steady, loyal and always there when you needed him. He was strong and staunch, yet humble, kind and generous beyond measure," he said.

"He always made room for a yarn and a laugh, or a quiet word when someone needed comfort."

"He was not a man who wasted words; the ones he shared carried wisdom, warmth and strength ... he shared lessons about life that stayed with you —leaving you feeling hopeful, grounded and ready to face what was to come next."

Tony Mundine's commitment to community lasted his entire life. Supplied by the Mundine Family. Source: Supplied / The Mundine Family

Mundine's nephew, Matthew Mundine, delivered the eulogy.

He reflected on Mundine's "quiet resilience, unwavering integrity and deep strength of character" that saw him become a "titan of Australian sport".

Acknowledging the legend's achievements in the ring, Mundine Jr said his "greatest victory" was the establishment of the Elouera Tony Mundine Gym and the Tony Mundine Hostel.

"He built far more than physical places — he built sanctuaries of hope," said Mundine Jr.

"For generations of community and young people, especially Aboriginal youth seeking direction, safe housing or a second chance, Tony offered a home away from home."

A "steady anchor", Mundine was a "deeply devoted" family man and a "loyal and steadfast" friend.

"Your fight may be done, but your victories are eternal — and your legacy will never fade."

Mundine's four children, Kelly, Natalie, Anthony and Kiah, also paid tribute to their father.

His youngest child, Kiah Tony Mundine Atkins, described her father as "positive, friendly, kind and happy", a man who "loved people" and deeply loved his grandchildren.

She recalled his cheekiness, his pride in his bright red car he constantly washed, and his funny sayings, "stone the crows, and everybody was a cowboy".

"Whenever I would ask my Dad, 'How are you, Dad?' He would say, 'I'm cruising like a butterfly'," she said.

"Keep cruising like a butterfly, Dad. I love you."

Mundine's eldest, Natalie Carr-Mundine, said her Dad had a special way of "touching people's lives".

"His legacy isn't measured by the titles he has won, or the fights he fought," she said.

"It's measured by the people he has inspired, and looking here today, he's inspired quite a lot of you."

Former boxer and Mundine's only son, Anthony Mundine Junior said he aspires to be like his father.

"If I can be half the man he was in his life, I'm doing alright," he said.

READ MORE Vale Tony Mundine, the champion who inspired generations

Four of Mundine's grandsons spoke, with Jade Mundine Atkins describing his Pop as their "world".

"I'm incredibly proud to be his grandson."

Family members, Lowanna Mundine and Birrpai Elder Uncle Heath Bugg also shared tributes alongside Nick Barnett, Mundine's closest friend of fifty years.

The memorial also heard from friends, colleagues and competitors from Mundine's boxing career, including ringside doctor Dr Lou Lewis, IBF World Super Featherweight Champion Barry Michael and boxing trainer and International Boxing Hall of Fame inductee Johnny Lewis.

Tribal Warrior CEO Shane Phillips shared reflections on the importance of the Elouera Tony Mundine Gym for Redfern's Aboriginal community, and Aboriginal Hostels CEO Shane Hamilton and Liz Simpson, who has managed the Tony Mundine Hostel for almost two decades, spoke about its impact on young Aboriginal men.

A young Tony Mundine ahead of his 1974 fight against American Bennie Briscoe. Source: Getty / Universal / Corbis / VCG

'A proud Bundjalung man from Baryulgil'

Born on 10 June 1951, Mundine was "a proud Bundjalung man from Baryulgil" — a small community on Bundjalung Country near Grafton in northern NSW.

He moved to Redfern at 15-years-old, following his talent in rugby league. But it was training in Ern McQuillan's Newtown gym that turned him to boxing.

Over 15 years, Mundine won 80 out of 96 fights and secured two Commonwealth titles. He remains the only Australian boxer to hold national titles in four weight divisions: middleweight, light heavyweight, cruiserweight and heavyweight

He cemented his status as a champion in 1974, when he challenged Argentina's Carlos Monzón for the WBA world middleweight title.

Mundine shared his gift, training others including his son Anthony Mundine Jr and grandson Rahim Mundine.

In 1986, he was awarded the Medal of the Order of Australia for his dedication and service to the sport of boxing and Aboriginal youth.

"Whether it was at the many national events and gatherings, or on The Block in Redfern, Coluzzi's Café in Kings Cross or in our family homes, Tony gave so much of himself to others," his family said in a statement after his passing.

"His legacy will live on through the many people he encouraged, mentored and inspired throughout his life."

title: Where's the snow? Could 2026 be Australia's worst season?
text:
IN BRIEF Snow depth has reached a record low with five ski resorts closing operations almost a month early.

The unusually warm winter is believed to be the cause of the short season.

Australian ski resorts are being forced to close a month early due to record-low snow depth.

Snowy Mountain's Spencers Creek hit a historic Australian low, recording a snow depth of 31.2 centimetres on 3 September.

The peak depth was 94.5cm on 13 August — the third lowest depth recorded in the region since 1954.

On average, peak depth is recorded in the first weeks of September. From the 1950s to the 1970s, the average depth in the first week of September was just over 180 centimetres — compared to the 120cm average from 2020 to 2025.

Deep Creek and Three Mile Dam also recorded record-low snow depths in 2026.

The 2026 ski season was the shortest on record, with five of Australia's ski resorts already shutting the slopes.

Victoria's Mount Baw Baw and Selwyn Snow Resort in NSW closed operations before the end of August — with Mt Hotham, Falls Creek and Charlotte Pass closing over the weekend.

The unusual winter warmth can be attributed to a multitude of weather behaviours, including El Niño, above-average sea surface temperatures, limited cold air in frontal systems and the ongoing impacts of climate change.

Australian Climate Council councillor and meteorologist Dr Andrew Watkins told SBS News in May it would be a warm winter.

"It's a winter of grabbing the skis when you can," he predicted.

He said Spring would come early with "clearer skies and more frosts".

title: Australian drone team arrives in Nepal as search for missing continues
text:
Australia is throwing more resources at search and rescue efforts in flood-devastated Nepal, with drone operators and victim identification experts joining the operation.

Australian rescue teams have landed in Nepal to join the search for those still missing after catastrophic floods swamped the country in August.

The 15-person specialist team landed in the capital late Friday, with additional support, including victim identification specialists on the way following a request for assistance from Nepali authorities.

A glacier collapse near Nepal's border with Tibet on 26 August triggered devastating floods across towns and valleys.

At least 36 Australians remain missing, with the federal government holding grave concerns for their welfare.

The death toll in Nepal is nearing 1300, with almost 4800 people still missing, including 601 foreign nationals, according to official figures released on Friday.

On the Tibetan side of the border, the death toll rose to 31 on Friday, an increase of 10 since the previous tally, according to Chinese state media.

It was not clear whether they were Chinese or foreign nationals. Some 531 people were reported missing, Reuters reports.

Foreign Minister Penny Wong confirmed on Thursday that local authorities would conduct searches in areas where many Australians were believed to have been staying.

She said Australian drone operators and incident management specialists would be sent to the region as part of a broader on-the-ground support team.

"I can indicate that after our inquiries that Nepali authorities have advised us that searches are being conducted in the locations identified by Australia, including (The Kailash Hotel) and the Royal Himalaya Hotel amongst others," Senator Wong told reporters.

The Disaster Assistance Response Team consists of specialists from the Queensland Fire Department and Fire and Rescue NSW.

Fire and Rescue NSW Commissioner Jeremy Fewtrell farewelled six remotely piloted drone operators and four incident management specialists as they travelled to Nepal on Friday.

"I was proud to farewell our team this morning as they began their journey to Nepal to support communities impacted by this disaster," Fewtrell said.

"Their drones will give search and rescue teams critical information about areas that may be inaccessible or too dangerous to reach from the ground.

"They have an important job ahead of them. I wish them a safe deployment and, most importantly, a safe return home."

The drone technology has AI capabilities that can help find victims, along with thermal imaging to identify anyone trapped.

DFAT is working with local authorities to establish the whereabouts and welfare of affected Australians and contact next of kin where appropriate.

Nepali authorities will also be given telecommunication data to help narrow the last known location of missing Australians.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers provided the latest update on the missing Australians on Friday, confirming that two more citizens were found safe.

It brings the number of Australians found since the catastrophic floods to seven, after five were confirmed safe on Wednesday.

Aid supplies aboard a Royal Australian Air Force plane also arrived in Kathmandu on Wednesday.

More than 1400 hygiene kits, 2200 solar lights and phone chargers were among the items.

title: The UN has backed a new world map that makes Africa bigger and the US smaller
text:
In brief The UN has voted in favour of adopting a new world map.

The new map updates the centuries-old Mercator projection to a "more accurate" scale.

The United Nations General Assembly voted Saturday to back a resolution spearheaded by several African countries to adopt a map that makes their continent bigger while shrinking North America and Europe.

Aimed at "a more accurate representation" of continental landmasses, the resolution was supported by 164 countries while the United States voted against it and six other states abstained.

The new map — known as the Equal Earth cartographic projection — "is a relevant option for improving the accuracy of the cartographic representation of the world," the resolution said.

It urges member states to adopt the new map in place of the traditional Mercator projection, which was designed for maritime navigation by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569.

Foreign Minister Robert Dussey of Togo, which drove the resolution, said maps "guide education, nourish the imagination, and influence collective perceptions."

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"They are therefore never neutral, when they present a distorted image of our planet, they risk perpetuating inaccurate representation that are passed down through generation."

The United States, however, slammed the resolution, saying such moves are "the reason this institution is losing its credibility."

"Instead of focusing on genuine problems ... this body is debating map projects from the 16th century and their role in promoting reparations and cognitive justice," US representative Yaryna Ferencevych said ahead of the vote.

'Distorted representation'

The Mercator projection focused on accurate depictions of the shapes and angles of land masses, but their relative sizes were often inaccurate — in part due to the challenge of rendering a three-dimensional globe onto a two-dimensional map.

It inflated northern regions and compressed equatorial ones, making Europe and North America appear much larger, while shrinking Africa and South America.

A group of cartographers launched the Equal Earth projection in 2018. It makes Africa, Latin America, South Asia and Oceania appear much larger.

The Mercator projection has been the default map of the world since the 1500s, but it greatly distorts the size of many continents. Source: AAP / Mary Evans

"Equal Earth preserves the relative surface areas of continents and, as much as possible, shows their shapes as they appear on a globe," one of the cartographers, Bojan Savric, told the Agence France-Presse (AFP) news agency in 2025.

France — which co-sponsored the resolution in support of the new map — announced Saturday that it would abandon the Mercator projection.

In that map, "the United States, Russia and China take on a disproportionate visual prominence compared to Africa, Latin America or southeast Asia," while "Greenland appears almost as big as Africa," Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said.

"Changing maps obviously doesn't change the world," he said. "But correcting a distorted representation is already an act of truth."

The initiative comes as France is seeking to improve relations with Africa, particularly in former colonies with which it has prickly ties.

In a savvy move that will see it vault from explorer to producer, Aureka Limited has tabled a binding agreement to acquire a producing Victorian gold mine and a strategically vital processing mill in a low-cash, scrip-heavy deal. The transaction lands squarely in the middle of a renewed wave of mergers and acquisitions in the Australian gold sector, where the market is tending to reward near-term production and cash flow over long-dated development stories. Under the terms of the deal, the company is set to acquire 100 per cent of High Grade Holdings (HGH), the parent company that owns the Fiddlers Creek gold and silver mine, along with 100 per cent of Vanning Resources, the operator of the 42,000-tonne-per-annum Wedderburn gold processing mill, for a base consideration of $8.9 million. Aureka Limited’s acquisition includes the operating 42,000-tonne-per-annum Wedderburn gold processing mill near its other gold projects in Victoria. The dual purchase has been structured as a majority-scrip transaction, comprising just $2.5 million in cash and $6.4 million in Aureka shares issued at 12 cents a pop. Aureka will also reimburse $500,000 in rehabilitation bonds. To fund the play, the company has locked in commitments for a two-tranche placement to raise A$5.65 million, which it says was supported by its significant shareholders. A matching share purchase plan to raise $1.5 million will also be offered to existing shareholders. The centrepiece of the deal is the Wedderburn processing mill, one of only six licensed gold mills in Victoria. With operating infrastructure relatively scarce in the state, control of a plant with stated spare capacity and a licence for external tolling could prove a strategic coup.

‘A low-cash majority scrip transaction at a compelling price-this is a transformative deal for Aureka.’ Aureka Limited managing director James Gurry The mill currently processes high-grade ore from the Fiddlers Creek underground mine, which restarted production in 2025. Aureka due diligence showed HGH has been generating positive monthly free cash flow since the second quarter of this year, just nine months after first production. During its fiscal 2026 ramp-up, the operation churned out 416 ounces of gold from ore with an impressive average head grade of seven grams per tonne (g/t). Recoveries averaged 86 per cent and hit a high of 91 per cent, producing a concentrate with a gold grade of about 70g/t, which is then sold under an existing offtake agreement. Notably, the deal also includes significant exploration upside on the acquired ground. The Fiddlers Creek mine lies within the Percydale goldfield, which has a history of producing over 700,000 ounces of gold. The surrounding tenure contains six kilometres of mineralised structure and more than 600 historical workings, with multiple parallel quartz-reef zones that have never seen a drill bit. As part of the deal, Aureka has committed to drilling at least 1800 metres on the acquired ground. Notably, the ASX has confirmed that Aureka will not need to re-comply with listing rules. HGH will have the right to nominate one non-executive director to Aureka’s board to ensure continuity. Up to a further $2 million in performance payments could be payable over three years if key milestones are hit. These are tied to cumulative production hurdles of 900 ounces of gold within 12 months 2500 ounces within two years and 4000 ounces within three years. An additional milestone concerns the delivery of a JORC-compliant resource for Fiddlers Creek, for which Aureka has yet to report an estimate.

The company is currently drill-testing extensions to Irvine’s 358,000-ounce Resolution Lode and says that, despite 59 kilometres of drilling since 2107, the geological understanding is still in its infancy, leaving plenty of blue sky for further growth. A key advantage of the new deal lies in the proximity of Aureka’s 56,500-ounce Comstock project at St Arnaud, which sits less than 50km from the Wedderburn mill, potentially providing a clear pathway to market for a second production source. The St Arnaud goldfield itself is a well-endowed region, with historical production of 400,000 ounces of gold at a stunning average grade of 15g/t. The company’s wider regional tenement holdings also include the Jubilee gold project near Ballarat and the Morning Bill gold and base metals project. Billionaire mining and media scion Ryan Stokes is the new chairman of the company that owns the Seven Network along with The West Australian and Triple M, becoming the fourth person to hold the role since the corporation was created via a merger at the beginning of the year. Stokes’ father, Kerry, stepped down as chairman of the company in February after engineering the merger of his TV and newspaper empire, Seven West Media, with radio company Southern Cross Austereo. Ryan Stokes is the new chair of the company that controls Seven, The West Australian, and numerous radio stations. Brent Lewin It has been a tumultuous start for the merged company. A number of executives from the Seven side of the business were ousted before the Stokes family took back control in a series of moves culminating in Monday’s announcement that Ryan Stokes would succeed Teresa Dyson, a longtime family associate, as company chair. The longtime controlling shareholders of Seven had their control of the company halved in the deal. Two weeks ago, the Stokes family bought back into the company for the first time since the transaction, with their Seven Group Holdings entity – which also owns mining equipment company WestTrac and machinery hire firm Coates – upping its stake in Southern Cross from 20.2 per cent to 23.2 per cent.

Ryan Stokes is also chief executive of Seven Group, and while he has been a director representing the group’s shareholding for some time, it is widely known that he does not share the same love for the family’s media assets as his father. Alongside the Seven Network, the company wields significant influence in WA through West Australian Newspapers, located where the Stokes’ mining business largely operates. The company also owns the Triple M and Hit radio networks, and the LiSTNR digital audio platform. Less than a year ago, the companies announced the deal which would result in Kerry Stokes retiring, Southern Cross chair Heith Mackay-Cruise taking over as chair of the combined company, and Seven boss Jeff Howard stepping in as chief executive. All three have since left the company’s management team and board, and the company is expected to formally rename itself under the Seven banner in the coming months. These platforms are now worth tens of billions of dollars and are growing exponentially. So far, they are not licensed to operate in Australia – in the case of Polymarket, it has been explicitly banned by the Australian Communications and Media Authority. Prediction markets offer odds on future events: the results of sporting matches, whether or when something will occur, what Donald Trump will say in a speech. People buy contracts in the outcome, and the price – or perceived likelihood of something happening – is set by the market. The companies dress this up as a financial product, but it is effectively just wagering. Live betting is allowed, and it’s where the action happens. USTA chief executive Craig Tiley, who ran the Australian Open for two decades until he left earlier this year. Getty Images If that is the future, the future is already here in New York. As the tournament began, new USTA chief executive Craig Tiley, formerly the long-time boss of Tennis Australia and tournament director of the Australian Open, announced a multi-year partnership making Kalshi the official prediction market of the US Open.

Advertisement

“We’re relentless about keeping tennis at the cutting edge of global sports innovation and fan connection,” he said. “Partnering with Kalshi gives us an opportunity to pioneer that next generation of fan engagement while ensuring the integrity of our sport.” Kalshi chief executive Tarek Mansour said tennis was one of the fastest growing sports on the platform. In August, Polymarket became the official prediction market partner for the ATP, the body that runs the men’s tennis tour, covering about 20,000 matches per season. The deal includes exclusive streaming rights, meaning Polymarket users can watch matches live through that platform, along with real-time data, side-by-side with betting options (or “opportunities to trade”). In any given stadium at the US Open, a healthy number of fans will be monitoring the match through a prediction market. Getty Images Polymarket’s head of sports business development, Ari Borod, noted tennis was a “natural fit” for prediction markets because of how momentum shifted point-by-point. That created “opportunities for expectations to change in real time”.

Advertisement

Related Article US Open Why this week could bring an end to the great American tennis chase And prediction markets enable real-time wagering on highly specific outcomes: who wins a set, the exact match score, total number of games, you name it. The US Open has even started sending push notifications to people’s phones about match predictions, “presented by Kalshi”. On the grounds, it was not difficult to find prediction market enthusiasts in the throng. Outside centre court, a man was walking around with a Kalshi microphone and camera, interviewing punters. Among every group of young men that this masthead approached, at least one – typically most – were avid sports gamblers. “It’s fantastic, absolutely fantastic,” said Jordan Levy, a 26-year-old New Yorker, who prefers the sports betting website DraftKings. “Tennis is honestly my favourite sport to bet on. You’re only betting on one guy … to me, you have a better chance of winning.”

Advertisement

Levy says he is up a few thousand dollars since the tournament began. He and his friend Josh Russ have bets on as we speak – for Jiri Lehecka to beat Stefanos Tsitsipas, and for Ben Shelton to prevail over Denis Shapovalov (Lehecka lost, but Shelton won). Just because someone is betting does not mean they are gambling away their entire savings. Gornbein, who said he wouldn’t be here unless he could play the prediction markets, says he is down about $US12.50 (about $17.30). His friend Adam Meitus, also 23, says he has lost $5 – although he struggles to name the player he was just betting on. Josh Russ (left) and Jordan Levy at the US Open. They use sports betting websites and prediction markets such as Kalshi and DraftKings while at the tournament. Michael Koziol But overall, the amount of money at stake is considerable, especially as prediction markets are still relatively new, even in the US. Kalshi’s website shows just over $US11 million (about $15.3 million) was traded on the Lehecka-Tsitsipas match by the time it ended. As it entered a fifth set on Saturday, a match between Taylor Fritz and Francisco Cerundolo had eclipsed $US8 million ($11.1 million). People have already wagered $US21 million (almost $30 million) on the tournament’s eventual winner. Most people bet responsibly and say it adds to their enjoyment of the experience. Obviously, the dangers of gambling addiction are well known. But there can also be impacts on the players from gamblers who turn ugly when things don’t go their way.

Advertisement

American world No. 3 Jessica Pegula said during a post-match press conference that it was a tricky matter. The International Tennis Integrity prohibits players from entering any sponsorship deals with betting companies. Tournaments have no such qualms. “We get a lot of negativity from people that use stuff like that, bettors – whether you win or lose, it doesn’t even matter sometimes. We get a lot of hate for it on social media,” Pegula said. “So, it’s tough when you see that and they’re a big sponsor behind the court, or they’re on TV. American world No.3 Jessica Pegula said prediction markets were inevitable, but she was uneasy about official partnerships. Getty Images “I don’t really know the best way to deal with it, just because it’s kind of the inevitable. It’s everywhere, it’s not really going away any time soon – especially when I look at other sports. Betting is a big part of keeping fans engaged. I go back and forth with that one.” Other players, or former players, are leaning in. Five-time grand slam winner Maria Sharapova, who retired in 2020, is fronting an advertising campaign for Polymarket.

title: More than 200 staff stood down at collapsed developer Bathla
text:
Advertisement

More than 200 staff have been stood down from the collapsed Bathla Group after a weekend of crisis talks, as administrators confirmed construction on developments in Sydney would be suspended. Bathla said in a statement on Monday that it had reached a short-term funding agreement with five lenders to enable limited operations to continue for a further two weeks, but 213 staff had been stood down and “construction on other projects will be suspended today”. Drivers bring vehicles into Bathla’s Girraween headquarters for what appears to be an odometer reading as staff are informed of the latest developments. Janie Barrett The developer, which has major projects across Sydney and thousands of properties in the pipeline, collapsed into voluntary administration on August 24 owing dozens of creditors $3.4 billion and has been teetering on the brink of liquidation. Teneo senior managing director Stephen Longley, the administrator, said on Monday the immediate priority had been securing enough short-term funding “to maintain a minimum viable operating structure”.

Advertisement

“The arrangements agreed today allow us to provide the central support required for construction to continue on projects associated with the lenders participating in the funding package,” he said. “Significant work remains to secure the funding required to progress and ultimately complete all projects currently under construction. We will continue to work closely with lenders and other key stakeholders to pursue those arrangements.” More than 200 Bathla employees have been stood down. Janie Barrett The administrators said that final documentation was expected to be signed later on Monday but the amount and the participating lenders would remain confidential. Further updates were expected to be provided to customers, employees, creditors, subcontractors and other stakeholders as the administration progressed. Premier Chris Minns said on Monday that the state government was “in discussions with the administrator” and noted while payroll was met last week “we’ve got a bit of a way to run”.

Advertisement

“There is still prospect for either the breaking up of the company and other parties stepping in to grab a piece of it and complete the works,” Minns said. “So I think that there’s an important process to take place before a line of credit or public money is extended to the company. And the reason today is it’s not my money; it’s public money.” Bathla’s headquarters in Girraween, which appeared quiet after the announcement. Janie Barrett Minns said it was possible for third parties to take over parts of the company: “In which case, the administration process will work for those home owners.” “Not all major builders in NSW are financed the same way. You know, this is a very strange corporate structure involving a hell of a lot of debt, largely collected from private capital, private credit, not through the banks and traditional finances,” he said.

Advertisement

Opposition Leader Kellie Sloane said she felt for those who had lost their jobs and was concerned for the companies and subcontractors who were owed money. “You know this collapse isn’t just one company; it’s affecting so many people and so many potential home owners as well, up to a couple of thousand of them.” Related Article Exclusive

Bathla collapse Developer Bathla told to fix defects as it staves off liquidation One Bathla employee leaving the company’s Girraween headquarters on Monday said he had not been stood down, but other staff had been. He did not confirm how many employees no longer have work and said he remained “positive” about Bathla’s future. After the announcement, Bathla’s headquarters remained quiet, with the few staff spotted leaving the site keeping their heads down and declining to speak to this masthead.

Advertisement

Outside the building, the car park was full with every kind of vehicle, from utes to BMWs. About five people could be seen through the glass windows, typing on their laptop. The group’s director, Bhart Bhushan, was not seen at the building. One person leaving the building said they were not a Bathla employee but had been brought in to “fix stuff” before another company could take the headquarters over. Bathla is leasing the Girraween site. Related Article Property development He was the ‘Baron of Blacktown’ – then his empire fell apart On Friday, it was revealed that Bathla Group owed at least $3.4 billion and administrator Teneo told creditors that “positive discussions” were continuing with five of the company’s 43 lenders to gain funding to keep construction going. Bathla Group – and its 542 individual entities – entered into voluntary administration on August 24. Teneo was last week desperately negotiating with lenders to secure short-term funding to stave off liquidation.

Advertisement

Bathla has 45 projects under construction in NSW set to deliver about 2500 homes, but administrators said the developer also has a significant land bank holding, at various stages of development. The administrator is also seeking to prevent the suspension of Bathla Group’s building licences by Building Commission NSW, which issued the notice of intention after the company entered voluntary administration. If the developer goes into liquidation, the licences would be automatically cancelled. Later on Friday, the state’s building regulator hit Raj & Jai Construction, a related entity of Bathla’s, with a building work rectification order to fix seven serious defects at an apartment building in Seven Hills. title: NRL stars fear set restarts could decide a final. V’landys says they’re ‘not telling the truth’
text:

SportNRLNRL 2026 NRL stars fear set restarts could decide a final. V’landys says they’re ‘not telling the truth’ Dan Walsh September 7, 2026 — 12:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

ARL Commission chair Peter V’landys says players are “not telling the truth” amid a renewed spate of criticism for the NRL’s expanded set restart rules, with Roosters skipper James Tedesco warning that contentious ruck interpretations could decide a club’s season. Tedesco and Cowboys counterpart Tom Dearden were among the finals captains to most strongly echo Harry Grant’s criticism after Melbourne’s win over Cronulla on Saturday night. Loading That match featured 24 infringements and 26 errors. Grant, the Storm, Maroons and Kangaroos hooker, then said the NRL needs to work out “do we want to play touch football or rugby league?” The governing body’s widened six-again remit – which sees a new set called for ruck infringements or offsides beyond the 20-metre line – has been a talking point all year.

Advertisement

The RLPA has been especially vocal regarding fluctuations in the rules’ enforcement. Data collated by independent statistician The Rugby League Eye Test indicates that set restarts in the final four rounds have increased to an average of 8.4 per game. That is a rise of almost 30 per cent from the 6.5 set restarts averaged per game between rounds 14-23. V’landys came out swinging in response to critiques from the players at the NRL’s finals launch on Monday morning, all but declaring the rules will remain as they are for 2027 despite the game’s long-held policy of reviewing all on-field matters at the end of each season. As Tedesco reiterated the concerns of numerous players, coaches and fans that set-restarts are awarded on the run and ruck infringements are not properly explained by officials, V’landys offered a blunt dismissal. “I don’t buy that,” he said.

Advertisement

“The two six-again [infringements] are 10-metre compliance, and this year we have 98 per cent compliance on the 10-metre [zone]. So it’s proven that if you have a deterrent there on a six-again, players will abide by the rule … And the fans did not like wrestling. The players know when they’re trying to control the ruck speed. James Tedesco is the latest high-profile player to raise concerns over set restart rules. Sitthixay Ditthavong “I think that they’re not telling the truth if they believe (that) when they’re given a six again, they didn’t know what it was for. I mean, I think it’s pretty obvious.” Tedesco said he was less certain than ever on why some set restarts were awarded while he has been out injured and watching Roosters games from the sidelines. “And I understand the referees are working hard, but when I’m on the field it’s hard to get a clarification of why we’re getting pinged at the ruck, so we don’t know what we need to clean up,” he said.

Advertisement

“I understand Peter is very focused on getting the ruck speed right, but personally, there’s a lot of times I’m not sure why a six-again is called. “I don’t really know how we get things more consistent either, but it probably is something we need to be aware of in the final series. You can’t let the games be decided by like six-again or set restarts, but you worry that could happen.” Dearden’s Cowboys side have been involved in as many wild, high-scoring shoot-outs as any side this season, with the Queensland and Australian Test player pointing to the new six-again rules as a key influence. “Personally, I’m old school, and I think we had the balance of the rules right last year,” he said.

Advertisement

“I’m not a fan of changing the rules every year. I don’t really see the need to keep adjusting or making these significant changes; I’d like a bit more stability in the game.” Asked about the potential of set-restarts being reviewed or potentially wound back in response to widespread player feedback, V’landys said: “I always look at raw figures and raw facts. You can’t base things on gut feeling, or you’ve got to base it on the facts. And at the moment, the facts do not support us changing that rule.” Speaking specifically to Grant’s comments that “you don’t know what constitutes a quick play-the-ball or what constitutes a slow play-the-ball”, V’landys said he has the utmost respect for the Storm captain.

Advertisement

“But he’s got this one wrong,” V’landys said. Related Article Analysis

NRL 2026 Bennett the Bunny whisperer: How Wayne has unlocked Souths’ lost boys “I let facts speak for themselves, and when you look at the facts, the ruck speed is still the same as it was last year. “It’s around 3.5 seconds, and it remains that way. And look, some teams try to take advantage of the ruck and slow the ruck down, and at the moment the referees aren’t allowing them to do that. “Some teams try to get the ruck speed up at over 4 seconds, and it doesn’t sound much, but .5 seconds is a lot, and it does slow the game down.

“So we make no apology that we’re going to keep the ruck speed the same for both teams. So no team gets an advantage any more. “And the referees, in my view, have done a terrific job… the raw numbers don’t back up what Harry’s saying.”

title: Trump would plunge the US into crisis if he carried out his latest bizarre threat
text:
Advertisement

BusinessThe economyTrade wars Opinion Trump would plunge the US into crisis if he carried out his latest bizarre threat Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist September 7, 2026 — 11:58am

September 7, 2026 — 11:58am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Last Friday, Donald Trump threatened to stop all trade with countries that have trade surpluses with the US ... unless the US Federal Reserve Board cuts interest rates. It is doubtful whether Trump has the power to carry out that threat or whether the Fed would take any notice of it. He also doesn’t appear to appreciate that, if he were able to do what he threatened to do, the US would almost certainly be plunged into recession, if not depression. Donald Trump has shown off his erratic character and economic illiteracy once again. Bloomberg Trump posted the bizarre threat on Truth Social (naturally) after payroll numbers showed a better-than-expected number of jobs were added in August. “Lower the interest rates because the U.S.A. is a much stronger credit than it was just a short time ago! A STRONG COUNTRY MEANS A LOWER INTEREST RATE – IT’S A BETTER CREDIT...VERY SIMPLE!,” he wrote.

Advertisement

“We should have the LOWEST RATE of any country in the World, like the ‘old days’,” he said. The US, with $US40 trillion ($55.5 trillion) of government debt, a fiscal deficit of about 6 per cent of GDP and an inflation rate of 3.7 per cent isn’t a strong credit – it is a rapidly deteriorating one – which is why investors in US Treasury securities have been pushing US bond yields up to near six-year highs. Related Article Media & marketing The inside story of the downfall of a Trump-loving host at Fox News The Trump administration’s profligacy (he added more than $US3.8 trillion to the debt in less than 18 months), his inflation-generating trade war on the rest of the world and his real war in the Middle East have added risk premiums to the yields on US government securities. “LOWER THE RATE OR I’LL STOP TRADING WITH COUNTRIES WITH WHICH WE HAVE A DEFICIT, which the U.S. Supreme Court, in its ridiculous and very costly Tariff decision, strongly acknowledged “the President” has an absolute right to do. IT’S BETTER THAN TARIFFS! The Fed board, with its great new leader, must get smart -- – be PATRIOTS for a change. High interest rates put the U.S.A. at a very unfair disadvantage, and I won’t allow that to happen,” he wrote.

Advertisement

It’s not at all clear that Trump has the power to do what he is threatening. The US Supreme Court decision in February that he cites and which ruled his “Liberation Day” tariffs were illegal dealt with a particular piece of legislation – the International Emergency Economic Powers Act – and taxing powers, rather than deciding any questions about the authority the president might have under it or other legislation to simply ban trade with another nation. Trump would spark economic chaos if he carried out his threat. Bloomberg The legal status of the replacement tariffs Trump has subsequently announced (based on the questionable grounds of countries not doing enough to combat slave labour) is being challenged in the courts and has yet to be decided. The presidential authority over trade is one delegated, and limited, by Congress. And the power to ban trade with another country is reserved for declared national emergencies. The Trump administration might be accelerating the US economy towards a financial and economic crisis and national emergency, but it’s not there yet.

Advertisement

It would face a national emergency if Trump were to cut trade with the more than 90 countries with which it has a goods and services trade deficit or the more than 130 countries with which it has a goods trade deficit. Related Article Opinion

Donald Trump Trump is an outlaw. And the US system was not built for an outlaw in the Oval Office Maureen Dowd New York Times columnist Last year, the US goods trade deficit (Trump never includes America’s $US340 billion services surplus) was $US1.2 trillion. Given that those countries that have a trade surplus with the US would probably also import products from the US – the value of their exports would be greater than their trade surpluses – the value of all the trade affected by a ban would be considerably higher. What would happen if he stopped all trading with those surplus countries?

Advertisement

The US dollar’s role as the world’s reserve currency and the centrality of its financial markets (particularly its bond market) to the world financial system promotes imports of both goods and capital. It also effectively lowers their cost for US consumers and businesses while making its exports less competitive. Kevin Warsh is chairman of the US Federal Reserve: It is improbable that the central bank which, unlike the administration, is staffed by a raft of people with economic expertise, will pay any heed to Trump’s “threat”. AP The US consumes more than its poor savings rate can finance. It borrows from the rest of the world to complement its savings and help finance investment and consumption, with the dollar’s singular role lowering the cost of those borrowings. The US imports products that it either doesn’t have or can’t make at sufficient scale itself, or where the imported products are cheaper or are of greater quality or consumer appeal than those it can produce domestically. Some of its imports are components in the global supply chains for products or equipment that are largely manufactured or assembled in the US.

Advertisement

Related Article Exclusive

Interest rates ‘Closer to the red line’: The perfect storm keeping economists awake at night If the US were to shut off imports with those countries that have trade surpluses with it, it wouldn’t have the ability to quickly replace them with domestic production. It wouldn’t, for instance, be able to replace its imports of coffee, bananas, cocoa, tomatoes and other foods immediately, if ever, and it doesn’t have the domestic deposits of rare earths, or copper, or even semiconductors to meet its domestic demand. So there would be severe shortages of some products and massive increases in the prices of those products, and others. Manufacturing plants would close, and jobs would disappear because companies would lose access to global supply chains for the raw resources and intermediate products they rely on.

Advertisement

Almost inevitably, there’d be an exodus of capital from US financial markets. There would be a severe spike in the inflation rate – and interest rates – and a cost-of-living crisis that would dwarf the one Americans are now experiencing. Recession, or something far worse, would be inevitable. The impact could be exacerbated if other countries (which would also be adversely affected, but at least would be able to trade with each other) were to retaliate and block US exports. Regardless, a global recession would be likely. In the longer term, it is conceivable that Trump’s bans on trade might generate more US home-shoring of production, but that wouldn’t moderate the near term shock and, in any event, wouldn’t fill in the vacuum left by the ban on goods that the US doesn’t have the resources to produce. It is improbable that the Fed which, unlike the administration, is staffed by a raft of people with economic expertise, will pay any heed to Trump’s “threat”.

Advertisement

Trade is beyond the Fed’s dual mandate of controlling inflation and maximising jobs and, in any case, the central bankers would recognise the level of destruction and self-harm that execution of Trump’s threat would generate. Patriotism, for the Fed’s governors, involves trying to blunt the impact of Trump’s inflation-inducing policies. The US would face a national emergency if Trump were to cut trade with the more than 90 countries with which it has a goods and services trade deficit or the more than 130 countries with which it has a goods trade deficit. They’d also be acutely aware that while they might be able to provide the anchor point for the US yield curve – the federal funds rate – the rates that businesses and consumers actually pay are set by the market and, with the bond vigilantes re-emerging and bond yields spiking, their focus has to be on lowering the inflation rate. Trump’s unhinged Truth Social post is a sign of the increased anxiety within the White House as the midterm elections loom. He might be right to see those higher bond yields as a threat to Republicans and his presidential authority, but threatening a trade ban unless the Fed does as it’s told will only strengthen the Fed’s resolve to protect its independence and make bond investors even more conscious of the erratic character and economic illiteracy of the president and his policies and the risk, albeit remote, that he might actually try to do what he threatens.

title: Woolworths shopper demands answers about meat after 'strange' $22 steak discovery
text:
A Woolworths shopper has sworn off buying meat at the supermarket and is demanding answers after a discovery inside a cut of steak.

Customer Matt Zarb paid $22.74 for two $60-a-kilo eye fillet steaks at a Woollies store in Taree, NSW, as a treat for himself and his wife.

However, a romantic dinner took an unexpected turn when he started preparing the meat in his kitchen.

"This meat, when you cook it, as you pull it apart and it's still uncooked, it seems sticky," he said.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"There seem to be very thin blue strands in it. I put a knife into it, and it just fell apart, really strange. It pulled apart like a piece of fish."

Having worked at a restaurant before, the 61-year-old said he had never seen steak behave the way the Woolworths steak did.

"We couldn't believe it," Matt said, adding that he and his wife refused to eat the steaks and instead fed them to their dogs.

Matt said the steak he bought from Woolworths for him and his wife ended up being fed to their dogs. Source: Matt Zarb

However, on multiple instances, the supermarket has denied the use of glue for this particular cut of meat.

"Eye fillet steak is a very lean cut of meat with minimal connective tissue, which is what makes it so tender. This is why it is easy to pull apart when pressure is applied," a spokesperson previously explained.

What caused the fish-like texture?

Regarding the "flakiness" of the steak Matt bought, McCartney said, "the cooked meat appears to be separating along its natural muscle fibres".

"This can be influenced by the particular muscle, the direction in which it was cut, freezing and thawing, cooking temperature and the amount of connective tissue present," he said, adding that while it may affect the food's texture, it does not indicate the steak was glued together.

McCartney said "it is important to distinguish meat quality from meat safety".

"A steak may be less tender, contain more connective tissue or have a less appealing colour without being unsafe to eat."
